paragraphs.text: II. NOTES ON JOB, IN ONE BOOK.

And he had great works upon the earth: because he was working by means of those very works. They held a feast every day until their number was completed: this is a sign of charity. And he offered victims for them according to their number: we are to understand that particular confessions are like individual victims, but there is another sacrifice, for all people and for all sins, which signifies the Lord. Lest perhaps my sons have sinned and cursed God in their hearts: “lest perhaps” is well added, because he suspected that they had cursed in their heart. And behold, the angels of God came to stand before God: the soul’s disposition toward the truth could not be narrated except by speaking of it in some way in terms of time and place. And the devil also came with them: was “with them” said because he could not hear except through them? And the Lord said to the devil: Where have you come from? The reply to the question is the comparison of his past action with that from which he is permitted to do something afterward. But the question itself is the divine power, under which he is not permitted to do whatever he pleases (for in the thoughts of the ungodly there will be questioning), and it serves to make him manifest to us. But put forth your hand and touch all that he has: give power. Unless he blesses you to your face: an unfinished expression, that is, “if he does not bless you to your face once his possessions have been touched,” as though one should supply: “what do you command?” And the devil went out from the presence of the Lord: from consultation to action. And enemies came and captured them. According to the saying “who now works in the sons of unbelief,” he stirred up these men too. It should be noted how he had power over human beings and over the elements, but power given by God. Naked I came out of my mother’s womb: note how consolingly he speaks, although he mourned according to custom.

Behold, I deliver him to you; only guard his life: so that he would not presume he could take away his life. And he took a potsherd to scrape away the pus: this signifies that through the Lord’s passion the sins of those who confess are scraped away.

And the night in which they said, “A man is conceived”: some higher powers, who were able to know this. Let that night be darkness: so that it may no longer suffer what it has suffered; that is, let it be darkness, that is, let it be given over to oblivion. Nor let the Lord seek it from above: let it not be restored through immortality, that is, let mortality perish. Nor let light come upon it: the light of memory. But let darkness and the shadow of death seize it: this life, which is a shadow of future punishment. The sense is: let the righteous man, who is light, not see it, but let darkness see it, that is, sinners and the carnal tribulations of this life. And let them trouble it like the bitternesses of the day: the precepts of the good life, or the day of judgment, by which carnal people are troubled. And let everlasting darkness take that night. Let it not be among the days of the year: the righteous who are spiritual, who enjoy the sun and are greater. But let that night be pain: because it causes pain to those who love it. Nor let it be numbered among the days of the months: the righteous in the church, on account of the moon as the lesser light, to whom it is said: “And I, brothers, could not speak to you as to spiritual people,” so that Paul himself belongs to the days of the year. But let him who curses that day curse it: the Lord, who will curse those who love carnal things. Let the stars of that night be darkened: those who are eminent in sins. Let it remain and not come into the light: because they will not be converted, he says by way of prophecy. Because it did not shut the doors of my mother’s womb: the earthly city, which Babylon signifies; for the doors would be shut if the sinner were not praised in the desires of his soul. For why did I not die in the womb? Before I stood out before you through some action; for conception pertains to hope. I came out of the womb, and why did I not perish at once? In these words, then, we must understand the figure of one who had grown old in such desires. And why did knees stand ready for me? So that I might be made firm there. Why did I suck the breasts? Teachings that nourish toward wickedness. Now indeed I would be sleeping at rest: by dying to this world. With the honored kings of the earth: in the church. Who gloried in swords: hence the words “and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” Or with princes who had much gold: wisdom. Who filled their houses with silver: the eloquence of the Lord. Or like a miscarriage slipped from its mother’s womb: so as never to stand out. Or like infants who have not seen the light: who have not attained to any distinction. There the ungodly laid aside their fury: in death from this world. There those weary in body found rest: either weary in body, not in mind, or having reached the end of bodily things. They did not hear the voice of the exactor: this is the source of “the judge will hand you over to the exactor”; that is, their sins have been forgiven them, for he was speaking of the ungodly. The small and the great are there: I think this is well understood as said of one person, according to the saying that whoever humbles himself will be exalted. And the slave not fearing his master: either according to the saying “Do you wish not to fear authority? Do good,” or according to the saying “Perfect love casts out fear.” For why is light given to those who are in bitterness? The honor of sinners. And life to souls that are in sorrows? In the material of sorrows, that is, in sins. Who long for death, and it does not come to them: the attainment of the fruit of sin. Death is rest to a man whose life is hidden: either because it is lived before God or because it is known to few. But this must be taken of that death by which we die to the world; for in the other there is no rest. For God has shut him in: by not giving him over to the desires of his heart. For before my food comes groaning: tribulations come before the joy of God’s food. And I weep, hemmed in by fear: seeing that I cannot avoid what I feared. For the fear I dreaded has come upon me: adversities that come from God’s mercy for correction. Neither in peace nor in silence nor in rest: for the things on account of which he feared were false. For wrath came upon me: vengeance, under which the righteous man is scarcely saved.

The words of Eliphaz. But who will bear the weight of your words? Here, then, he says he is compelled to speak because he cannot bear what Job has said. Is not your fear foolish? For you ought to have been prepared for these things, if you were truly persuading others. Nor were you right to fear such things when you said, “For the fear I dreaded has come upon me.” And your hope and the simplicity of your life: as if it were the folly by which these things are thought to be good. The roar of the lion and the voice of the lioness: the devil himself and the city of pride, which the prophets often present in the manner of a beast as well. And the joy of the dragons is extinguished: of the proud and the treacherous. The ant-lion perished because it had no food: because at the end there will be no one for it to lure in and devour; for the godly will be separated from the ungodly. But here he errs, in that he took things he had heard prophesied about the devil to refer to Job. The ant-lion is to be understood either because both natures are in him, since he both seizes and secretly pursues the grain, which he keeps from sprouting by removing its eye; or because he rules over the greedy and those who lay up treasure on earth; or because he persecutes the righteous like ants that prepare food for themselves in summer for the winter, food on which he will not feed when the good have been separated from the ungodly. And the lion’s whelps are scattered from one another: the conspiracy of the princes of that city, who were born of the fellowship of that city and of the devil, has been dispersed; or else because they ravaged one another. Hence: “Nation will rise against nation.” None of these things would have happened to you: either those losses and the bereavement and the stroke of the wound; or else grief of mind would not have pierced you, because you would have comforted yourself as well, if you had spoken to others from the heart. Does not my ear receive great things from him? Because he says that what he is saying he says from revelation. And a spirit met me face to face: he wants it understood that he felt a kind of breath; for in what follows he denies that there was any form. We should remember that the Spirit also descended upon the apostles in this way. For what? Shall a man be pure before the Lord? Either he says he heard this, or he says he shuddered because no one is pure before the Lord; or else that he saw it thus because no one is so pure before God as to see God as he is. Here “pure” is to be taken in the sense of perfection, so that we may understand in a certain sense what he denied above, that a pure man perishes. If he does not trust against his servants: this happened when Elijah said, “Lord, they have killed your prophets,” and he says to him, “I have left myself seven thousand men.” For that did not mean that the seven thousand men were already pure. For prophets too have been called angels. And against his angels he found something perverse: either what is said against them or what they themselves say. Yet this can also be taken of true angels. But those who dwell in houses of clay: whose way of life is not in heaven. He struck them like a moth: either some corruption struck them like a moth, or God struck them, either by this moth or as a moth strikes, that is, secretly and from within, by corruption arising from themselves through carnal desires, that is, through dwelling in houses of clay. And from morning to evening they are no more: either they do not exist beyond this age, or from prosperity to tribulation; for punishment has overtaken them. And because they could not help themselves, they perished: when they have hope in themselves. They died because they did not have wisdom: the wisdom not to hope in themselves.

But call, if there is anyone to answer you: for an answer is given to those who are pure before God. For wrath kills the foolish man: the indignation by which a person is tormented, as though something had befallen him unjustly, while he does not consider that he is so impure before God that the angels have not deigned to answer him when he calls, or to show themselves to him. For whoever does not consider this is foolish and is slain by irrational wrath. Or else the fool cannot hear or see angels because he has been slain by wrath and killed by envy. But envy kills the one who goes astray: so that he imitates sinners. But I have seen fools putting down roots: “fools” here are to be understood as the ungodly, so that, conversely, a man’s wisdom is godliness, as is said in what follows. And let them be crushed at the doors of the weak: the humble, when these have been received into the chamber by the bridegroom and the foolish have remained outside. For what they have gathered, the righteous will eat: this can be understood both of the Jews, who gathered the prophecies which the Gentiles instead ate, and of those who, by doing, eat what others teach and do not do. But they themselves will not be delivered from evils: although they preach that these things should not be done. Let their strength be drained: the strength by which they are proud against the weak; let it be drained, so that it may now begin to toil. For toil does not come forth from the earth: that is, let them not complain about creation but about themselves. But man is born in toil: “is born” is said in the sense that each person passes from a quiet life into a toilsome one. But the vulture’s young fly very high: the vulture is well understood as the Lord, because from the height of prophecy he saw our mortality, on which he would feed when he descended, turning us into his body. So they are called “the vulture’s young” as they are called the sons of the bridegroom, and “flying very high” as having their way of life in heaven, so that they may be freed from the toil in which man is born. For they followed the voice of him who said, “Come to me, all you who labor.” “The vulture’s young” can also be understood in a bad sense as the powers of the air, which feed on deaths, that is, on sins. Since angels who are transgressors of this kind have not been brought down to the humility of the very toilsome mortality in which man is born, they are exceedingly proud, that is, they fly very high. Who gives rain upon the face of the earth: as if he shows mercy to those who confess. So that their hands may not accomplish the truth: let them not do what they promise in their eagerness to lord it over the weak. In the day darkness will meet them: as with the Jews, who did not recognize what the Lord was. Or let them grope at noon as in the night: just as, though they saw signs, they nevertheless doubted, some saying, “He is a prophet,” others, “He leads the people astray,” since they would not see even by lamplight. And let them perish in war: in temptations. And let the weak go out from the hand of the mighty: of the devil. But let there be hope for the weak; for those strong men seek their goods here. But blessed is the man whom the Lord reproves. In this, then, he errs, because he thinks Job suffers these things for his iniquities, whereas he is blessed precisely because, being reproved in this life, he has the possibility of correction. And in the seventh, evil will not touch you: the sacrament of the Sabbath. In famine he will deliver you from death; for he nourishes with the word and makes one firm against temptations. And in battle he will free you from the hand of iron: from the power of chains. From the scourge of the tongue he will hide you: so that you do not feel insults, not so that you do not suffer them. You will laugh at the unjust and the wicked: as wisdom will laugh at the destruction of the wicked. And you will not fear raging beasts: that is, you will not fear the Jews, because the Gentiles will obey you. These things are to be understood of the Lord. Eliphaz errs here because he thinks the things revealed to him are to be understood of Job, though the whole of it applies to the Lord. For you will have a covenant with the stones of the field: stones of the field, because among the Gentiles there was no ordering of the law that would make them like the stones of a building. For the wild beasts will be at peace with you: whether among the Jews or among the Gentiles. Then you will know that your house will be at peace: that is, the church. And your children will be like all the grass in the field: without withering. And you will come to the grave like ripe grain: to the passion. Behold, we have searched these things out thus: here the authority of this prophecy is confirmed. But you, know for yourself what you have done; for God has not unjustly permitted these things to befall you.

The words of Job. But, as it seems, my words are evil; for Job’s words do not come from impatience under the scourges, since they signify a grief not peculiar to Job, but one he felt for the whole human race. For the arrows of the Lord are in my body: the words of God, by which the soul is pierced when it is driven to confession. Whose fury drinks my blood: for they take away sin. For when I begin to speak, they goad me: for what I say, they compel me to say. For what? Will the wild ass bray in vain, unless it is seeking food? So that it suffers hunger for this reason, because it wanted to be free. Or does the ox low when it has food in the manger? Food for the ass is prepared by the labor of the ox, just as food for the Gentiles is prepared by the labor of the prophets and apostles, who were of course Jews. So these are the words of one who longs for food, that is, for help, not of one impatient of pain. Can bread be eaten without salt? As if it were said to him, “Why do you say these things in figures?” he answered: because if he said them in his own person, they would be insipid. Or is there flavor in empty speech? He calls the speeches of men empty, because the words of God are bread, but heavenly bread. So my soul cannot cease either: just as bread cannot be eaten without salt, so now I provide the ministry of the word of God, because of the saying “How will they hear without a preacher?” For I see my food as foul-smelling, like the odor of a lion: for my words are foul like a lion, either because of pride, through which boasters stink, or because those who embrace carnal things, who delight in their own words, have the stench of a lion. But if he would grant it, and my petition would come: by “petition” he means the thing he was asking for. And may the Lord grant my hope: for thus, trusting in the hope of the consolation that will come after tribulation, he is fittingly tested. He rightly says “hope,” because when the thing itself has come, testing will no longer be necessary. Let the city be my grave, upon whose walls I used to leap: he wants that fellowship of Babylon to be his grave, not so that it may bury him, but so that he may know that it covers as dead all who are in it, the city in whose stronghold and fortification, as it were, he used to take pride. I will not spare; for I have not lied. The words of my God are holy: because he said nothing other than what he heard from God, that is, as one prophesying about man in general, that he needs help in confession. For what is my strength, that I should endure? This is what his wound signified. Or what is my time, that my soul should hold out? Because people are terrified when death is imminent, so that they turn and confess to God the rottenness of their sins; he says that by considering this he is compelled to confession. Is my strength the strength of stones? Those who are hard and impenetrable to the darts of God’s words, who are not moved to confess. Or did I not trust in him? When it was well with me, that is, when I was immortal in the image of God. But help has departed from me: having become mortal by wishing to trust in myself. And the visitation of the Lord has despised me: according to what is said: “Or the son of man, that you visit him?” My kinsmen did not regard me: I became abhorrent to the angels. Like a torrent that fails: for mercy once flooded over me, and I dried up and was no fountain to myself. Or like waves they have passed me by: as if consolations were drink. Those who feared me have now rushed upon me: the devil with his angels. I have perished and become an exile from my house: either from the heavenly dwelling or from conscience; that is why he sat outside his house. Look at the roads of the Temanites, observe the paths of the Sabeans: he means those who trust in temporal things, in which he says that he, that is, the man whom he signifies, does not put his confidence. But now you too have risen against me without mercy: thinking that people’s happiness lies in abounding in carnal things, since they insulted him rather than sympathizing. But seeing my wound, be afraid: understanding what it signifies, fear future punishments. For what? Have I asked anything of you? Or do I need your strength? Because he is weak before the one who can save him. Teach me, and I will be silent: that is why they ought to have been patient toward his teaching, since they themselves could not teach him. But, as I see, you speak perverse words of a true man: by a true man he means the one who represents the person of someone doing penance by turning to God, whose words they called perverse. For I do not ask help from you: for the true man asks help from God; for the one who confesses is true. Hence: “He who does the truth comes to the light.” Nor will I endure the utterance of your speech: for he said that he endures God’s speech, by which he is instructed. Yet you have rushed upon an orphan: as far as you were concerned, you wanted to insult me, although you did not understand what it signifies. Because they ought not to have insulted even Job, whom they saw, he says “yet.” But now, as you look on, be at leisure for me: since you have nothing to teach me. And again stand by justice: because at first they thought they were compelled by justice to speak. For there is no iniquity in my mouth; and did not my throat meditate wisdom? He says that he did not accuse God, but introduced a man accusing his own iniquities, as his speech above was understood. This is what he calls the meditation of wisdom.

"Is not human life on earth a trial?" Here he now shows more openly whose figure he was speaking for above. He calls it a trial in the sense of a stadium for a contest, where a man either wins or is beaten. "And is his life not like that of a day-labourer?" That is, of one who looks for a temporal wage. So the life of those who look for the fruit of their righteousness in the future is not a life on earth. "Or like a slave who fears his master and has got hold of a shadow?" This is signified by Adam hiding from the face of the Lord and covering himself with leaves, which make shade. Man got hold of this shade when he had abandoned God. "Or like a hireling who waits for the wage of his work?" This one differs from the one above in that the former already had temporal things, while this one longs to have them. "So I too have waited through empty months": he called them empty in keeping with the shadow, that is, temporal goods. "And nights of pain have been given to me": nights in which the light of wisdom is lost and there is matter for punishment. "If I sleep, I say: When will it be day? And if I rise, again: When will it be evening?" This is when a man, at leisure, longs for business, and in business longs for leisure. "But I am filled with pains from evening until morning": from the time he fell away from God. That is why God, walking in the evening, sent them away. This signifies the willing [?], for whom there is no hope of a remedy except in the morning. Of this morning it is said: "In the morning I will stand before you," that is, when after the judgment God will be revealed to the righteous in the morning. That is also why the Lord is buried in the evening and rises in the morning. So he can compare this life to the morning star. "And my body is clotted with the rot of worms": with a multitude of worms. "I pour out clods of earth, scraping off the pus": the squeezing out of desires, or of the cares of confession. The wicked delight in this, because they turn into an occasion for sin what others confess through penance. Hence the dogs that licked the sores of Lazarus. "And my life is slighter than my speech": for I do less than I say. "Remember, then, that my life is breath": that is, in spiritual hunger. "And I will not return to visible things. The eye of the one who sees will not recognize me": because I shall be changed. We are to take "the one who sees" here as the devil, who looks on in envy. "Your eyes are on me, and I cannot stand": for you kill in me the carnal life in which I used to live. "Like a cloud cleansed from the sky": either cleansed by the sky, as we speak of something being cleaned with iron, so that he meant here that help came to him from heaven to cleanse him; or else that it is no longer a cloud but is thinned out into pure air, as if cleansed by the rays of the sun, so that the darkness of flesh and blood is not in heaven. For flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God, when this corruptible body has put on incorruption and death is swallowed up in victory. "For if a man goes down to the underworld, he will not come up again": remember this, then, so that you do not go down. "And he will not return again to his house": that is, to his rest. "Therefore I too will not restrain my mouth": by confessing, while there is time. "Am I the sea, or a dragon?" For you have not driven me back as you have the wicked or the devil. "For you have set a guard over me": so that I may not be stirred into turmoil, just as the sea has its bounds. "For I said: My bed will comfort me": the carnal things in which he used to rest. "And I will take comfort for myself on my couch": but I ought to look to you for my comfort. "You terrify me with dreams and astound me with visions": with the tribulations of this life, which are dreams just as the good things of this life are dreams. "You will release my soul from my spirit": because of visible terrors, from which the soul will be set free if it fears to come to them. "And I have driven my bones back from death": for my bones would have gone to death had I not been frightened by these things and become stronger and patient, which is what the firmness of the bones means. "For I shall not live forever, so that I should bear it patiently": I corrected myself by thinking of the shortness of life and the fear of death. This is why the devil cannot be converted: he does not die but is condemned. Hence fear is the beginning of wisdom. "Depart from me, for my life is empty": because I cannot bear trials. "Or is it because you have set your mind on him?" Because he is rational. Hence the saying: "But we have the mind of the Lord." By the gift of reason he means the reach of the understanding. "And will you judge him in rest?" As worthy of rest. "How long will you not release me?" He was bound by tribulations. "Nor let me alone until I swallow my spittle?" That is, until, in pain and under the scourge, I restrain and swallow down the flowing of pleasures, warned by tribulations. "If I have sinned, what can I do to you?" The sense here is: if I have sinned, I can do nothing to you. Or perhaps men trouble you by their speaking? Then you, who know the mind, why did you make man so that he would speak against you and be a burden to you? But if a man's sin harms you neither by deed nor by word, why do you not forget his sin, but rather purge it, unless the things said above are to be referred to your goodness? "For what is man, that you have exalted him?" His friends did not understand these things and thought he was finding fault with God. For if you do not send me trials so that I may restrain my flowing impulses, and so take care of me, what other reason is there for you to rebuke man? He cannot harm you by sinning. Or do you feel his speech as a kind of opposition, when you know the human mind and could certainly have avoided creating what opposes you? "And why have you not forgotten my iniquity?" If these trials are not for this reason, that they should benefit me, so that all of it comes from your goodness, why do you rebuke me? "But now I shall go into the earth": for though you purge my sin, it still remains for me to go into the earth through bodily death. "In the morning I shall wake, and I shall be no more": in this earth.

The words of Bildad the Shuhite. "He has put their iniquities into his hand": he put them into his hand either for punishment or for reckoning, as debtors; that is, he showed them to be sinners. "And he will restore to you the life of righteousness": the life that is owed to righteousness, that is, the blessed life. "And your former things will be very small": compared with the later ones, which will be without end. "Or will these not teach you and tell you?" For some have greater authority. Here too, since he is about to speak of Christ, he recounts things he has heard, just as Eliphaz recounted a revelation. "Can the rush grow green without water?" In the same way the wicked will wither without the mercy of God. "While it still stands in its root and is not cut down?" If it has no water. "Before any grass drinks, does it not wither?" Unless it drinks; for the wicked man never grew green beforehand. "And his tent will be filled with spiders": useless works. Now he seems to be speaking of the Jews and the Lord. "And if he props up his house, it will not stand": either the holy scriptures, or the hope of the Lord's promise, or the kingdom itself. "And when he has begun, he will not continue": in following God. This is what happened to the Jews, who began but did not follow. "For he is moist before the sun": rotting with the flux of carnal things. "Before the sun" means under tribulations, so that "before" signifies "under," as when we say: "Do it before me." "And from his rot his shoot will spring up": for if they had not been so wicked, the Lord, who was born of them according to the flesh, would not have been exalted through his passion. "He sleeps among heaps of stones": for the elders will crucify him. "And he will live among the pebbles": the humble, among whom were the apostles. "If he is swallowed up, the place will disown him": if he hides that he is the Son of God, it will be said that he is not the Son of God. So he must make himself known, for in this place divine things cannot be known. "But from the earth another will spring up": either the Lord by rising again, or another kind of godly people, that is, Christians. "For the Lord will not approve the innocent." Or: will he not reject him? Or else: the wicked man will not approve the innocent? "Nor any gift": that is, the sacrifices the Jews had. "But he will fill the mouth of the truthful with laughter": of those who confess. "And the tent of the wicked will not endure": either the temple itself or the kingdom.

The words of Job. "Truly I know that it is so": that is, that he repays me these things according to my iniquities. But this is not as you suppose; it is because no one is righteous in his sight. "They will not answer him one in a thousand": for he will convict them in everything. "Who brings the mountains to old age, and they do not know it": that is, to weakness, as in: "I have grown old among all my enemies." "Who overturns them in his anger": in his anger he overturns them, that is, so that they find something other than what they were seeking, since whoever exalts himself will be humbled. "Who shakes the world from its foundations": through the calling that was made, by which those who were eminent in the world were shaken. "And its pillars will be moved; who commands the sun, and it does not rise": so that either wisdom is not understood, or those who wrote are not, as in: "Seal the book." "Who alone stretches out the heaven": the church, which is properly the seat of God, and which he stretches out through the whole world. "Alone" signifies the unity of the Trinity, for certainly all things were made through the Son in the Holy Spirit. "And walks on the sea as on land": "as on land" means firmly strengthening the church in the world, or subjecting sinners to himself; he does not sink among them, because he does not give way to their temptations. "If he passes by me, I shall not see him. If he is higher than I am, or brushes past me in his speed, I shall not recognize him": so it is necessary that he both adapt himself to my weakness and not abandon me. "For if he hands someone over to death, who will turn him back?" For he hands over to death when he either passes by or passes on, so that he is not known. This is the death of the soul: not to know God. "For his anger cannot be turned aside": the anger of others can be turned aside by someone more powerful. "By him the other things under heaven are made subject": except heaven itself, that is, the rational creation. For if it had subjected the other things to itself, it would never be punished through the things it had subjected. But because God subjected them to it, it is punished through them whenever it offends the one who subjected them. "And even if I am righteous, he will not hear me": if I ask him while relying on my own righteousness. For comparing it with the unchangeable and everlasting things that are with him, he will not hear me, as being unrighteous. So I need his mercy. "I will ask for his judgment": because I cannot judge myself to be righteous. Hence the saying: "But I do not even judge myself; it is the Lord who judges me." "But if I call and he does not hear me, I will not believe that he has heard my voice": when I ask for his judgment, if he does not hear me, I will not believe that he ever heard me; for he heard me for hidden reasons, not because of the merit of my prayer. Or else: I will not believe that I am not heard now, for at some time I was heard. Or thus: if he grants what I ask, I will also believe that I have been heard; for if I do not believe, then even if what I ask comes about, I have still not been heard. So the sign of being heard is the faith of the one who asks. "Lest perhaps he crush me in a whirlwind?" That is why I seek his judgment, so that he may not crush me in a whirlwind. "For he has multiplied my tribulations without cause": their cause was hidden from me. Or else this is the voice of one confessing, admitting that he has not been corrected by God's scourges and so may be crushed by a whirlwind, as by a greater punishment. "For he does not let me catch my breath": so many are my tribulations. "Indeed, because he is able, he prevails": he wins, so that I do his will, not mine. "And even if I am righteous, my mouth will speak impious things": if I think myself righteous. "Yet my life will be taken away": though I do not know whether I have acted impiously, yet my life will be taken away, so that I suffer what I do not want or do not do what I want. "There is one thing I have said: anger destroys the great and the mighty": that is, tribulations come upon men for this one reason, so that no one should think himself great and mighty, relying on his own strength. "For wicked men will be in a great death": not in a moderate one, such as the righteous are in when they are afflicted and mocked by the wicked. "The earth has been handed over into the hands of the wicked": either the body of the righteous, not the soul, when the wicked persecute them, or when the wicked man is allowed to rule. It can also be understood of sinful man handed over into the hands of the devil because of his mortality. "In making his judgment, he covers it": either the judgment on the wicked man himself or on the righteous; for in this present time it is covered. Or else by this very act he makes his judgment on him, that is, he punishes him by hiding his providence from him, as in: "In the greatness of his anger he will not seek." Or he vindicates the righteous man by hiding his judgment, that is, his providence, from the man who persecutes him, so that the persecutor is caught all the more tightly in the snares of sin through going unpunished. "And if it is not he, who then is it?" This can be understood of the Lord, who was mocked, whose earth, that is, whose body, was handed over into the hands of the Jews, and who in making his judgment hid his majesty. If it is not he, who then is it who does greater things than he did? Or thus: if God does not make judgment on the righteous or the wicked, who can? "But my life is swifter than a runner": he calls men who depart from righteousness runaways, like the younger son who set out for a far country. "Or like an eagle flying in search of food": from the higher things in which rational souls are by nature blessed, that is, the works of righteousness, they have stooped down to earthly pleasures. "And if I speak, I forget while I am speaking": this is an idiom. Just as he was attached to outward things, so the soul, as it goes out toward the things outside in its desire to enjoy the creature, forgets the Creator within. "Bowing down on my face I shall groan": for pains follow that turning aside. "I tremble in all my limbs": the fear by which he begins to run back. "And since I am wicked, why have I not died, and toil on?" Supply "I know." Or he says he toils because he has not died to wickedness. "And though I were cleansed with clean hands": either God's hands or his own, that is, good works through regeneration. "You have plunged me deep enough in filth": brought down into this mortality. "And my garment has abhorred me": immortality, with which we long to be clothed over. But because we cannot be in this corruption, he says: "My garment has abhorred me." "For you are not a man as I am, that I might answer you back": to a man I could prove my righteousness, but in your judgment I am found unrighteous. "Would that there were an arbiter between us!" He seems to blaspheme, unless he is understood to be longing for that mediator between God and men, through whom he might present his prayers. For in this way he, standing between the two, hears and rebukes man, since the Father has given all judgment to the Son. "And one to rebuke and one to hear between the two." "Let him take his rod away from me": let the fear of the law pass away, so that I may be joined to him in the freedom and love of adoption. "For I am not with myself": because I cling to the things that are outside.

"I will bring words against myself": these are the words of one who is confessing. "And I will say to the Lord: Do not teach me to be wicked": do not tempt me beyond what I can bear, and do not let anything happen to me that would persuade me to impiety. "Or is it good for you if I act wickedly?" It is not good for you if I act wickedly, so you have not made me this way unjustly. "Because you despise the work your hands have made?" If you despise any work of your hands. "Have you paid heed to the counsel of the wicked?" But not the impiety that is visible to men. And: "Have you paid heed to the counsel of the wicked?" Not because it pleases him that they act wickedly. "Or do you see as a man sees?" Because you certainly do not see as a man sees, you have paid heed to the counsel of the wicked. For there is an impiety that you alone see and that men do not see. "Or is your life a human life?" That is, short, so that you could not judge about what is everlasting. "And you have searched out my sins": for things hidden from men could not be hidden from you. "For you know that I have done nothing wicked": for as far as men are concerned I have done nothing wicked. "But who is there to rescue me from your hands?" The hands of one who judges. You judge as God, since you see even the impieties that man does not see. "But afterward you changed and struck me": that is, he himself had changed, not God. A changed man feels that God has changed, just as eyes changed by long darkness feel that the sun has changed. "Remember that you formed me from clay": so I need your mercy. "You will turn me back into earth": through death, which is the penalty of sin. "Did you not milk me out like milk?" Because he showed mercy even to men who were [already] mortal, when he formed men from men out of a formless beginning. "Since these things are in you, I know that you can do all things": because they are of such goodness that they produce even fleshly substance. "And if I sin, you will keep watch over me": either so that you do not destroy me, or so that my sin is not hidden. "And if I am righteous, I cannot catch my breath": in the sight of men, for you see sins that are hidden from men. "For I am full of disgrace": in your sight. "And I am caught like a lion for slaughter": there is a sin of pride that is hidden from men, since it can creep in even into praiseworthy deeds. "But again you change and torment me most cruelly": after the penalty of sin, by which man was made mortal. He is speaking of the tribulations that men suffer in this life. Many tribulations strike suddenly and disturb the quiet of this mortal life, when it is in good health or secure in its possessions, however temporal; and he had attributed that quiet to God's mercy. "Renewing my torments upon me": because mortality itself is already a torment, and from it other tribulations arise. "Why then did you bring me out of the womb?" Out of obscurity into notice, which alone is the occasion of greater misery when it is overthrown; he mentioned this birth above as well. "And would I be as though I had never been?" Entirely unknown. Hence the saying: "He calls the things that are not as though they were," that is, in respect of obscurity. "Or is not the time of my life short?" For it is not because my life is long that I have not died, since the time I live is certainly short. "Bear with me, until I rest a little": after the mercy by which you made me from mud; after you changed me and struck me with mortality, and comforted me with that very mortality; and then . you trained me with tribulations. Bear with me, then, so that I may rest in you before I go to the punishments from which there is no return. For from the ones he mentioned above there is a way back, if a man turns to God. He wants to rest before he goes to eternal punishment, precisely so that he may not go there. It is as if we were to say to someone: "Correct yourself before you are condemned"; for once he has corrected himself, he will not be condemned. "Where there is no light, and no seeing the life of men": for the life of men is where the true light is, which enlightens every man. The land of the living is one thing, the land of the dying another.

The words of Zophar the Minaean. "Or will an eloquent man be thought righteous?" For he thinks that Job abounds more in words than in deeds. "Blessed is the man born to a short life": he throws back at him his own statement, which he wants understood as wordy and empty talk. "Since there is no one to contradict you": because when Job spoke, no one contradicted him. "But how would the Lord speak to you?" Rather, say the things for which God might have mercy on you. "For it will be double upon you": by rebuking and by comforting. "And then you will know that the Lord has repaid you justly for your sins": after correction, enlightenment follows. "Or will you find the footprint of the Lord?" So that you would want to find fault with God. "Heaven is high; and what will you do?" To discover the mysteries of heaven. For you ought not to find fault with one whose works you do not comprehend. "Who will say to him: What have you done?" For even this will have been rightly done if God has done it, since he cannot do anything except rightly. "For he knows the works of wicked men": this is not the work of one who is wicked [?]. So he wants it understood that this man, whom he thinks wicked, has foolishly found fault with God, for that is how he took Job's words. "But a man wavers in his words": now God pleases him, now God displeases him, whereas with God there is firmness. "And a man born of woman will be like a wild ass in the desert": through desire for freedom he cannot bear a master or a tamer. "And stretching out your hands to him": so that he may accept your works. "If there is anything wicked in your hand": he has repeated the same two things, but in reverse order. "And let no iniquity remain in your house": by this he meant the heart. "For then your face will shine like pure water": the conscience. "Like a wave that does not pass by, and you will not be afraid": unless it touches everyone in this life. "And your prayer will be like the morning star": it will go before the enlightenment. It is as if these things too, which concern the prophecy of the holy city or the people of God, are spoken as things heard or revealed, just as they were spoken earlier by his friends. "And many will entreat your favour": all these things are about the church.

The words of Job. "But a righteous and blameless man has become a laughingstock": this is to be understood of the Lord. The sense is: so it is no wonder if I too have become a laughingstock to you. "And his house, that it should be laid waste by the wicked": the church, by persecutors. "Nay rather, let no one who is wicked trust that he will go unpunished": because judgment begins at the house of God. "As though there will be no inquiry into them": let them not trust in this. "But ask the four-footed beasts, whether they will answer you": he rightly makes inquiry of the wicked, then, because they could have recognized the Creator from his works and ought to have worshiped him; for they should not have needed to be taught by an answer from creatures, since they had received reason, by which to know these things. "If the soul of all living things is not in his hand": from this, then, it is known that he created all things, because the soul of all living things is in his hand. "And the spirit of all the flesh of man": of all human flesh, that is, of the rational soul. "For the ear judges words": just as sense judges the things of sense, so the spirit judges spiritual things; and the spirit, since it is in the Lord's hand, ought to have recognized the works of the Lord. "In long time is wisdom": not, surely, in long time, but with the Lord, from whom it is to be sought. "If he destroys, who will build?" He destroys because of his power and shuts in because of his wisdom, so that one does not attain to it. "If he withholds the water, he will dry up the earth": the water is wisdom itself, and the earth is man. "And if he sends it forth, he will destroy, overturning the earth": for when many have been made wise, sinners will be thrown into confusion. "Who leads counselors captive": for he brings under his yoke those who consult him. "And he has cast the judges of the earth into dread": either the Jews, or Pilate, or those who judge with an earthly mind. "Who sets kings upon thrones": that is, the apostles. "And he girded their loins with a belt": that is, with continence. "Who sends priests away captive": so that they are led by men; and the Jews are signified. "Who changes the lips of the faithful": he changes them for the better, so that they rely not on their own righteousness but on his grace. "And he knew the understanding of the old": he who is pleased by the understanding of the old. Hence the saying: "You are known by God," the opposite of which is: "I do not know you." And he rightly began from faith and arrived at the gray hairs of understanding. "Who reveals deep things out of darkness": by opening up the prophecies. "And he brought the shadow of death into the light": that is, he caused this life to be recognized as the shadow of death. "Deceiving the nations and destroying them": they thought they were harming the church of God, when they were harming themselves; this is to be understood of the ungodly. "Laying the nations low and leading them into the way": into humility, like that donkey. "Reconciling the hearts of the princes of the people of the earth": reconciling to himself either the Jews or the kings of the earth, who at first persecuted the church. "But he led them astray into a way they had not known": by undermining the works of the law, so that they would be understood plainly; this is why he seemed to them a sinner. Darkened by this error, they are like a drunkard.

"And I will reprove in his sight, if he wishes": so that he may reprove himself; and this belongs to confession. "And you are all healers of the wicked": for you cannot heal the good with your consolation. "Hear, then, the rebuke of my mouth": against you. "And before his face you bring forth deceit": when you want to seem righteous, which you are not. "Or do you withdraw yourselves from becoming judges?" Can you pretend not to notice and refuse to judge, because what I say about you is true? "For even if, doing all things, you are added to him," that is: even if you keep all the commandments, he will find something in you to reprove; for no one is righteous in his sight. "And if you secretly admire persons": your own, by justifying yourselves not only before men but even before yourselves. "But the body is of clay": so that you may fear, at least from considering your own frailty. "Taking my flesh in my teeth": I will not spare myself, so as to reprove not only you but also myself. "And I will place my soul in my hand": to be examined, so that I conceal nothing; or so that I may count up my sins. "Though he who is mighty, who has also begun, should slay me": though he should slay my sins. "Yet I will speak and reprove myself before him": I will not justify myself by hiding my sins. "Behold, I draw near to my judgment": so that I may judge myself, as though man's very righteousness lay in not sparing himself in confession. "Then I shall not be hidden from your face": as sinners are hidden. "Take your hand away from me": so that there may be nothing in me that needs chastising, and that there may be love in me. "And let not fear of you terrify me." "How many are my iniquities?" From this it can be seen that he said, "I will place my soul in my hand," for the purpose of reckoning. "Or do you think me your adversary?" Since I am surely weak, it is as if you feared this: that if I were justified I would be your equal, when I am but a leaf. So there is some hidden cause, since it is not this. "And you have laid on me the sins of my youth": so that this is the reason why he says his sins are hidden from him, because he was proud, which is a sin of youth. "And you have put my foot in the stocks": in the bond of mortality. "And you have observed the roots of my feet": my desires. "I who grow old like a wineskin": so that I cannot hold new wine, or be patched with new cloth, like a garment eaten by moths.

"For man born of woman is short of life and full of wrath": that is, of punishment. "And have you made this one come into judgment before you?" Mortal as he is, he still has something for which to render account; for what he is able to do is required of him, however very little he can do. "For his months are numbered with you": for by the very fact that he is temporal he is convicted of sin; for you had made him eternal. "Depart from him; let him rest": this is according to the opinion of the carnal and natural man, for whom this life is the whole of good. And so he wants to be spared, so that he may enjoy this life. "For a tree has hope": these words are to be spoken mockingly. For surely man has more hope, which carnal people refuse to believe. "But a man, when he has died, is gone": this too is ironic. "For in time the sea will diminish": for afterward it is filled again. He is speaking of those places where there is an ebb and a flow, or else of the fact that all shores imperceptibly diminish and increase according to the hours of the moon; that is, when the moon rises, either for us or for others, the sea grows until the moon reaches mid-heaven, and from then on it diminishes. "Until the heaven is no more, he will not be sewn together": to the new, that is, to heaven itself. "Oh that you would keep me in the underworld": so great is the hope of resurrection that I would wish to be free already even of these uncertainties of life. "And hide me until your wrath had abated": hence the saying, "Hide yourself for a little while, until the wrath of the Lord passes," that is, until this mortality passes and we come to the resurrection. "For if a man dies, he shall live": for this is not life. "When the days of his life are completed": then he will live. "Then you will call, and I will answer you": obeying you without the hindrance of mortality. "You have sealed up my iniquities in a bag": to repay them to me. "You have noted whether I went astray against my will": you have noted even this. But to go astray unwillingly is the punishment of sin. "And indeed a mountain, falling, flows away": so too man fell from his height and firmness. "And a rock grows old in its place": as man does in his kind and condition. "And by the washing of frequent floods": as if man too has been brought to such wasting, worn away by the frequent floods of desires. "But you have destroyed the hope of man": he has made a series of steps: from mountain to rock, from rock to stones, from stones to sand, because carnal people suffer these diminishings. And he rightly now said "you have destroyed." "For you have driven him to the end": to consumption, so that this hope in which carnal people rejoice may perish. "You have changed his face, you have sent him away": when the image of God in him was banished. "And though his sons be many, he does not know it": because he dies, even though offspring are propagated. "But his flesh grieved over him": that is, man grieves carnally and mourns in a natural way over this condition of his; for the spiritual man knows that even though the outer man is decaying, the inner man is renewed day by day, because he feels this happening within himself.

The words of Eliphaz the Temanite. "And he has filled his belly with pain": for the spirit of knowledge rather heals from pains by consolation; but you, who fill your belly with pain, do not answer with the spirit of knowledge. "Have you not also cast off fear?" You did not fear God, saying such things against him. "And you have chosen the tongue of the wicked": with which men curse. "For what? Were you born the first man?" Since you are so proud. "Or were you formed before the hills?" Mountains too are to be understood by the name of hills, that is, before all the powers, the mighty spirits. "But there is among us one both old and very aged": there is someone among us who knows even what we do not know. "What has your heart dared? And what have your eyes endured?" They have hoped. "For what is man, that he should be without fault?" As you yourself have said. "If there is no faith in his saints?" Because of the uncertainties of the times, by which they are often deceived, so that they say many things and do not do them. "And the heaven is not clean before him?" This stands for those who dwell in heaven; or else heaven stands for the saints themselves, because God dwells in them. "What wise men have spoken, and have not hidden from their fathers": because the apostles preached even to the Jews. "To them alone the earth was given": to inhabit. "Nor does any stranger come upon them": neither holy man nor angel; that is, they will possess it in security. "When they think they are already at peace": he speaks as if he thinks this happened to Job himself. "He does not believe he will turn back from darkness": he does not believe so as to be turned from his sins. "And he is destined to be food for vultures": for the powers of the air, which feed on the deaths of sinners. "Like a captain in the front line he will fall": he is bold and does not bear tribulations. "Who has lifted up his hands against God." Or: "because he has lifted up"? "And he has run insolently against him": by doing the contrary of what he commanded. "With the thick neck of his shield": relying on his own protection. "Because he has covered his face with his fat": through fat, that is, through the exaltation of his pride, he hid God from himself. "And he made a halter upon his thighs": so that he would be bound by his lusts, a bond by which he would be led to death. "For what they have prepared, others will take away": even the earthly kingdom itself, or whatever temporal hope, which the righteous will receive together with the whole world. "And he will not grow rich, nor will his substance endure": that is, the ungodly man's. "He will not cast a shadow upon the earth": that is, he does not flourish. "But the wind will dry up his stock": temptation. "His cutting will rot before its hour": before he hopes. "Let him fall like the flower of the olive": let him fall away from peace; or because better things follow these, as fruit follows the flower. "For the death of the ungodly is a testimony": a sign. "And fire will burn the houses of those who take gifts": for these are the ungodly, who put temporal gifts before righteousness. "He will conceive groans in his belly": the things he hopes for serve to his punishment.

The words of Job. "I have heard many such things": not only what you are saying. "Comforters of the wicked, all of you": you can comfort the wicked, because they imitate you, but not the good. And it is a vocative; for I have heard nothing good from any of you. "For what? Is there order in words of the spirit?" Of pride. "Or in what will it be troublesome to you?" Even though you do not love what you say. "I too speak according to you": as you deserve. "If your soul were put in place of mine": if you were suffering what I suffer, I would be speaking in words, not deeds; so it is worthless to speak of what you do not do. "For if I speak, I will not grieve with the wound": you show yourselves prudent neither in speaking nor in keeping silent. For the wise, even when they speak, share in grief as they console; either, speaking in their confession, they grieve over their own wound, or when they are silent, they keep silent prudently. "But now he has wearied me and made me foolish and rotten": so that I should not speak against you, God has broken my pride, so that, made foolish, I may become wise. "You have seized me, and I have become a testimony": you have convicted me of my sins, and I am a witness against myself. "And my lie has risen up against me": when I seemed righteous to myself. "I have answered against my face," that is: "I will set you before your own face." "Using wrath, he cast me down": he rightly said "using wrath," for he does not suffer it; but he cast him down as one who was proud. "He gnashed his teeth at me": he rebuked me, so that teeth are to be taken for words. "The arrows of his pirates have fallen upon me." These are the powers of the air, which God uses and to which he gives leave, so that the good may be exercised or the wicked punished; and they are pirates because they lie in wait for those sailing on this sea. "With the keenness of his eyes he rushed in": he did not overlook my sins; as it were, he nodded that I should be punished; for he is like a light to the punishers, showing them whom they are to punish. "The sight of him was ruin to me." Or else: he made me see my sin, for before it had not been brought home to my awareness like this. "The mighty God struck me sharply, and at the same time they converged upon me": for as God struck, the angels of Satan converged. "When I was at peace, he tore me apart": he tore me away from peace itself, or from my very self, so that I was torn to pieces by adversaries and by those opposed to him. "And holding my hair, he tore it out": through my sins he divided me against myself. "He set me up like a target": for them to shoot at, as a target is usually set up for archers to aim their shafts at. "They surrounded me with lances, hurling them into my kidneys; they did not spare": this is because of the carnal desires that he says were driven into him by evil angels through evil persuasions. "They poured out my gall on the ground": so that I envied earthly goods in those who abound in them. "They cast me down with a great prostration": lest we should understand a carnal prostration. "They sewed sackcloth to my skin": the inward sins, by which he recalls that he had lived among good things. "And on my eyelids is the shadow of death": I want to see, and carnal habit hinders me. "Let not the earth cover the blood of my flesh": that is, lest, if my prayer should be unclean through wishing for earthly things, a heap of earth be added on top of the bond of mortality, which he signified by the name of blood; that is, lest through earthly desire I be buried under the greater calamities of voluntary sin, on top of that natural sin which comes from the mortal condition. "And let there be no place for my cry": let the merit of my prayer be shut off. "And now, behold, my witness is in heaven": he seems to be speaking of the Lord, because he had not yet come down to earth. "And he who knows me is on high": because of his sharing in mortality. "Let a man be judged with the Lord": let the Lord come, so that a man may be judged alongside him, as John was with Christ. In judging between them, one understands how great the difference is between a perfect man and God made man. "As a son of man with his neighbor": the Lord, having taken up a man, came to the one who had fallen among robbers. "For the numbered years have come to me": that help comes to me through Christ in the fullness of time. "And I will enter the way by which I shall not return": the way of renouncing the world.

"I have failed, shaken in spirit." The order is: I have failed in spirit, shaken by toils. "I pray to be buried, and it does not befall me": that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. For we groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over, that is: let us be changed rather than die. Which surely does not happen, however much a man desires it; for he owes death by the condemnation of sin. "I offer prayers with toil. And what have I done?" I have achieved something by my petition. "Strangers have stolen my goods": he signifies immortality itself, of which he is despoiled, he who was left half-dead by robbers. "Who is this?" Who is to come to my help; he signifies the Lord. But he says "Who is this?" because he was to be among men in such a way that he could scarcely be told apart from them. "Let him be bound to my hand": by the bond of love, so that he may guard me and lead me where he will. "Because you have hidden their heart from understanding": you have hidden the heart of those who did not recognize him. "Therefore you will not exalt them": because they were not humble, they were blinded and could not be exalted by the humility of Christ. "Let evils be announced to a part": because blindness has come upon part of Israel; or because the things Christ announced seemed evil to them, so that they said, "He leads the crowds astray"; or it refers to what was announced through the prophets about the blindness of Israel. These things did not befall the whole, but a part. "And the eyes over their sons have wasted away": in wonder at the miracles, about which it was said: "If I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out?" "But you have made me a byword to the nations": the man you redeemed, that is, the church, of which the nations would speak, or which would speak to the nations. "And I have become a laughingstock to them": either to the nations, when they disparaged it, or to the Jews, who spoke to the nations. "My eyes are darkened by wrath": the eyes of the church, that is, the apostles, were darkened when they were not understood by those who were to be punished with this penalty. "And I have been fiercely assailed by all": for Jews and Gentiles alike assailed the church. "And the truthful were amazed at this": either at why power was given to the ungodly against the church, or at why the gospel was not recognized by the ungodly. "But let the righteous rise up against the enemy": he who falls for a time through persecutions, so that afterward he may rule over the unbelievers. "And let the pure of hands take boldness": the boldness of hope, so as to confess Christ even in persecution. "For I do not find truth in you": for grace is necessary to all, Jews and others alike. "And the joints of my heart have been torn apart": so that I may not conceal my sins. "They have turned night into day": the ungodly have. Hence the saying: "Woe to those who call good evil and evil good, who put darkness for light and light for darkness." "If I endure, the underworld will be my house": if I put up with myself so as not to confess my sins. "I have called destruction my father": I will not be a son of life; but God called [him]. "My mother and my sister, corruption": because they cling inseparably, like kin. "For what hope is there now for me?" Understood: if I endure. "Or shall I see my good things?" The things by which he was led astray; he refused to be converted and put up with the sinner.

The words of Bildad the Shuhite. "And the light of the ungodly will be put out": so do not wonder if your light too has been put out, as an ungodly man's. "His light was darkness in the house": the brightness of his house; that is, they were either the devil or the antichrist. "And the lamp over him will be put out": a small and earthly light. "Let the lowest take his substance": what he wanted to have, let the humble have. "For his foot has been thrust into a snare": for he himself was caught by persecuting the Lord. "He will strengthen the thirsty against him": so that those who hunger and thirst for righteousness may overcome him. "His cord is hidden on the ground": by which he is to be caught; that is, the things that are, as it were, granted to him. "And his capture is in the paths": by which he passes. "Let pains destroy him round about": on every side. "And let many around his feet come into the straits of hunger": many who follow him or who serve him. "Let the branches of his feet be eaten": of his teachings, that is, by which he goes. "Let health be broken off from his dwelling": the tranquillity of this life. "And let the necessity of the royal cause hold him": the occasion of his punishment, which will serve the glory of God, and for this reason his desire is now permitted him. He speaks of a royal cause because he will boast that he is the Christ. "Let it dwell in his tent in his night": let the necessity of the royal cause, the craving for tyranny, torment his conscience; "in the night": in the punishment of his blindness, when he is condemned. "His fair things will be sprinkled with sulphur": the things he delighted in, let them be burned up with a foul-smelling fire. "And his harvest will rush down from above": from God. "And let his name not be in the face of the streets where it was": let it be taken from the people's memory. "And let him not be recognizable among his people": let him come to such abasement that he is not recognized by his own. "Nor let his house be restored under heaven": for some will be restored. "But let others live among his people": let his people be subjected to others.

The words of Job. "And you break me down with words": you weaken me, you who ought to have comforted me. "Know only that God has done this to me": it is before him that I can be convicted of sin, not before men. "And he has surrounded me with his rampart": a ditch runs around the walls; by this I was forced into confession. "Behold, I laugh at reproach and do not speak": he is speaking of the usefulness of confession, because if he chose to laugh at his sin and not speak it out, he would cry out and not be heard. "He has set darkness on my face": he has taken the light of my face from me, which is what happens to those who have turned away. "And he has taken the crown from my head": the spiritual dignity that wisdom gives. "And he has torn me apart on every side, and I am gone": I held all things, and he took them from me, as against the power of holding all things that I had received. "And he has counted me as an enemy": he judged me as if I would harm him if I were his equal. "And they have surrounded my tent": my heart and conscience. "My brothers have withdrawn": in hope of my correction, because they are brothers, although at first they scorned my correction and followed those who urged on them what was alien to them, that is, ruinous. "And my friends have become merciless": in spiritual ills. People who feel for their neighbours instead mock them in these, though they would not mock them if they were in bodily ills. "And those who knew my name have forgotten me": they do not recognize me, because I have been changed. "The neighbours of my house and my maidservants": those with whom I shared secrets; flatterers, who withdraw from one who confesses to God, for they are the ones said to play the maidservant. "I called my servant, and he did not answer": either the body or those who served him in evil. "My mouth was pleading, and I was entreating my wife": as if saying, "Why are you sad, my soul? And why do you trouble me?" That is, wanting her to consent to him. "I called coaxingly on the sons of my womb": those he had begotten by persuading them of the hope of this world. "And those I had loved rose up against me": in that life. "In my skin my flesh has rotted": through love of the things perceived outwardly, my inner parts have rotted. For it would surely be a trifling matter, if we take it literally, as though he had had the itch. "And my bones are in my teeth": my firmness and strength lie in words, not in deeds. "Have pity on me, have pity on me, O friends": he seems to be asking the angels to intercede for him, or certainly the saints, to pray for a penitent. "For it is the hand of the Lord that has touched me": he says that he was touched by the Lord's hand so that he might feel the pain of his wound, which had been without feeling for him. "Why do you persecute me as the Lord does?" You loathe me and shudder at me as the Lord does; or you rebuke me when I am already confessing. "Are you not sated with my flesh?" You do not rejoice if I live carnally. "With an iron stylus and lead?" So that, as lead yields to an iron stylus, the hearts of men may yield to my words. "Or carved in the rocks for a testimony?" So that those who are firm for preaching the gospel may learn them. "For I know that he who will release me is eternal": because he can restore me. "Of which I am conscious in myself": because I deserved those things. "Which my eye has seen and not another's": that is, no one knows what goes on in a man except the spirit that is in him. "And all things have been accomplished for me in my bosom": in the inner parts where no one sees, that is, in the conscience. "But if you should also say, 'What shall we say against him?'" According to what is said even to the spiritual: "Looking to yourself, lest you too be tempted." "And shall we find the root of the matter in him?" So that we may convict him from his own words. "For wrath will come upon the wicked": he calls wicked those who exalt themselves over sinners and think that they themselves could never be such.

The words of Zophar the Minaean. "For you do not understand any more than I do": he turns to the others who were consoling Job with him. "I shall hear the instruction of my shame": indirectly he wants Job to hear the instruction of his own shame, for then he can also attain the spirit of wisdom. This is a customary way of speaking, as when we say, "It is good for me to be careful, for otherwise it will go badly for me," when we want someone else to be careful. "Have you known these things from of old?" Since the ages began, you have known these things. And he thinks that Job is ignorant of these things, as an ungodly man. "The eye will see and will not add": for he will not be seen. "May the ungodly one destroy his sons": that is, may the devil destroy either his imitators or those he has led astray. "And may his hands be burned with pains": may they be tormented by his works. "His bones are filled with his youth": he is proud of his strength. "He will hide it under his tongue": being deceitful, he will not show it, so that he may make use of it secretly. "He will spare it and not let it go": loving it and unwilling to be without it, he does not pursue it; or: the Lord will spare him, and because of this impunity he will not let it go. "And he will hold it in the middle of his throat": as something that delights him. "And he will not be able to help himself": he will not free himself by it. "The gall of an asp is in his belly": in his inward parts, in secret, he harbours a malice that does harm. "Riches unjustly gathered will be vomited up": with torment of the inner parts and anguish of heart. "An angel will drag him out of his house": whenever his hidden deeds are revealed through tribulations. "And he will flash with the fury of dragons": so that he who was hidden at first, once betrayed by tribulations, now openly flashes with the fury of dragons. "May the tongue of a serpent kill him": may the devil lead him astray. "And may he not see the milking of the herds": the yield of the sheep; that is, may he not do the works of righteousness, so as to realize that by them he can be redeemed. "Nor the pastures of honey and butter": good works done with love, with cheerfulness of heart and generosity in the giver; for butter is rich milk. "He has laboured in vain and to no purpose": because he does not understand that with these riches he should do the works that belong to mercy. That is why the Lord too is said to eat butter and honey, because these are offered to him in his lowly ones. "Which will be like something hard that cannot be chewed or swallowed": the hard thing is iniquity or pride. "In his desire he will not be saved": because he desired wicked things. "There will be nothing left of his food": his desires pass away. "When he thinks he is filled, he will be straitened": the fullness of one's desires brings not so much satisfaction as distress. "If somehow he may fill his belly": such need will come upon him that he will doubt whether he can fill his belly, although these things are surely sought precisely to drive need away. He said this because the more a man has, the more he desires. "And he will send upon him the fury of his wrath": because he did not see to doing good works. "May a bronze arrow wound him": an everlasting one. "May a javelin pass through his body": may temptation pierce him, so that he is wounded both by what he hopes for and by what he leaves behind, as if run through from chest to back. "Lightnings in his tents": sudden terrors in his thoughts. "May a stranger harm his house": the devil, who comes from outside to tempt, since a man also has temptations of his own. "And may heaven uncover his iniquities": the judgment of heaven. "And the possession of his goods is from the Overseer": God will bestow these on him.

The words of Job. "And let me not have this consolation from you": the consolation by which you think that one should rejoice in temporal goods, though they are common to the godly and the ungodly, and that whenever someone is wicked he is punished here by their loss; whereas Job says that these goods remain with the ungodly right up to the grave, and that they are not punished by means of them. "For what? Is my chastisement from man?" My chastisement is from God; so he can also comfort me, not you. "Or why should I not be angry?" So do not comfort me in this way, for I certainly see the prosperity of the ungodly. "Look at me and be amazed": as though I were speaking empty words. "For if I remember, I am troubled": going back from the state of mind he is now in to his former one, he confesses the indignities of human life. "And my flesh is gripped by pains": I suffer in the flesh. "Why do the ungodly live?" He asks them for the reason, because they were saying that the ungodly are punished here. "And their sheep endure as into old age": how can they last into old age? For they will not exist forever. "Yet their goods were in their hands": he did not take those goods away from them, though they said these things. "No indeed, the lamp of the ungodly will be put out": their temporal brightness, even if not in the way these men understood it. "May his sons be deprived of his goods": the goods he persuaded them of, namely temporal ones, whether the sons of the antichrist or of the devil. "May his eyes see his own slaughter": he indicates that those who rejoice in this prosperity do not understand it either, but in the future it will be brought home even to the awareness of the ungodly. "For he has no will in his house after him": because in their conscience they did not reach the Lord in their tribulations. "Though the number of his months has been cut in half": although he worshipped God for the sake of the present, yet he did not also hope for the future, which is the full number of months. "For does he himself judge murders?" Because when the ungodly have persuaded others to ungodliness through love of carnal impieties, they surely kill them for the world to come. Yet men do not judge such murders; God alone does. "This one will die in the strength of his simplicity": he seems to be pursuing the subject of hidden murders, mentioning one man who is generous and another who is greedy, because people who are wealthy and generous are also thought to be good. "His bowels are full of fat": he has gladness. "And their marrow is poured out": the marrow of the bowels, because he does not keep his goods to himself but spends them either on himself or on others. "Therefore I know that you press me boldly": for you do not speak with consideration. "Because you say, 'Where is the house of the prince?'" Of the ungodly or of the proud; because they thought that goods are taken away from such men here, although many have even ended their lives full of them, to be punished by means of them. "And where is the covering in the tents of the ungodly?" Their honour. "Ask those who pass along the road": those who do not take delight in the road but pass along it. "And you will not fail to recognize their signs": either the signs of the ungodly that passers-by give when they say what will become of them, or the signs by which the ungodly are recognized. "Who will declare his way to his face?" No one but the Lord boldly declares his way to the face of the ungodly man, because he himself answers him. "And yet even the Lord himself was led to the grave": so the reward of godliness is not to be hoped for here. "And he kept watch over the heap": for he himself rose before the heap of those who rise. "The stones of the torrent were sweet to him": those whom the world did not overturn, that is, his disciples. "And after him every man follows, and before him are countless ones." Or: after him every man, that is, one man, and before him countless ones who are now reckoned among the number of men. Or: after him the crowd of believers, and before him the patriarchs and prophets. "How then do you comfort me in vain?" By urging present goods or present evils.

The words of Eliphaz the Temanite. "Is it not the Lord who teaches understanding and knowledge?" As though Job had said that God does not judge rightly; when God certainly could be faulted only by an understanding superior to his, though it is he who gives understanding to man. "And will he come into judgment with you?" So that you might be compared with him. "Your light has been turned into darkness": your dignity. "And water covered you as you slept": a flood of tribulation came upon you when you felt secure. "Does he judge through a cloud?" As if he could not see through a cloud. "Clouds are his hiding place, and he will not be seen": what is on earth is hidden from him. "And he goes round the circuit of heaven": the shape of the sky, not the earth. "Will you then keep the path of the world?" As if Job thought that God does not care for human affairs. "Because they were seized before their time?" Before their time in their own view, for they thought they would remain forever; or at least before they attained wisdom. But these friends of Job said this because they had heard it, not because they understood these things. "And the thought of the ungodly is far from him, and he fills their houses with good things": the thought of the ungodly is far from him because he does not act as the ungodly man hopes, that is, as if ungodliness pleased him or he did not see it. "The righteous saw it and laughed": understanding it; although these men did not understand, thinking that the ungodly receive their due here. "And the blameless mocked them": the ungodly.
