"Be hard, if you endure": be patient, that is, endure hard things. "You will put iniquity far from your tent": from your conduct or way of life; although these men say this in a carnal sense. "And you will set it on a mound, on the rock": in contrast to what he said: "a river flowing down their foundations." "Because he humbled himself": the light itself. "And you will say, 'He was lifted up in pride'": against the proud. "Rescue the innocent, and you will be saved by the cleanness of your hands": do not falter in good works, for God cares for human affairs.

The words of Job. "And indeed I know that the rebuke comes from my own hand": from my sins. "And my hand has grown heavy upon my groaning": you struck me so that I might feel pain. "And come even to his throne?" That I might be so holy as to attain to the number of those who are his seats. For then I can speak and hear what is true; which is also why the heavens are called holy. "And I may know the pleas he will speak to me": the accounts of his reasons, by which he shows that he judges all things justly. "And I may perceive what he declares to me": being by then close to him. "Will he contend with me in great power?" So as to resist me by force. "By no means. Only let him not abuse me in terror": because of my sins, which make me afraid now; while I am in terror, let him not abuse me. "But when I come to him": in that freedom in which I shall be counted among those of his throne, I shall love all things, and his power will not resist me; although now he can abuse me, as I am a sinner. That is: let him do with me what he wills, even to my punishment, yet justly. "For truth and rebuke are from him": that is, he does not rebuke unjustly. "He brings my judgment to its end": even if he corrects me now, he will make it plain afterwards. "For if I walk first, afterwards I shall not be": let me not hope arrogantly, let me not despair faithlessly; that is, let me not turn aside to the right or to the left. Hence the words: "If I ascend into heaven, you are there," and "Who can drive me from there?" and so on. "What he does on the left I shall not grasp": he repeats what was said before. He says that one given over to temporal things, on the left, will not grasp it. "He will turn to the right, and I shall not see": therefore I ought not to be on the left. He said "he will turn" because he himself is among spiritual things, from which I turn away if I am on the left. "But he knows my way": so that even if he leads me through tribulations, I may follow. "He has tested me like gold": in temptations. "I shall go forth in his commandments": let me come out of my darkness, but in his commandments. "But if he has so judged": to test me like gold through tribulations. "Therefore I hastened to him": because he afflicted me, I left temporal things behind and hastened to him. "And when admonished I was anxious about him": so that through these bodily punishments I might escape eternal torments. "Therefore I shall be troubled at his face": I shall be troubled now, so as to be on my guard, thinking of the judgment to come, where he will be revealed. "And the Lord has softened my heart": he credits even this fear, by which he guards against future punishments, to God's mercy. For he would not know that punishments and darkness are coming upon the wicked unless the Lord softened his heart through present tribulations; in contrast to the passage where God hardens Pharaoh's heart.

"Why have the hours not been hidden from the Lord": "why" meaning "wherefore," or "therefore." "They have overstepped the boundary": Christ. "And they have turned the poor aside from the right way": so that the poor would either imitate them or conclude from this that there is no divine judgment, because they saw that the malice with which these men harmed them, abandoning justice, went unpunished. "The meek of the earth hid themselves together": together with those who turned aside from the right way, the meek hid themselves so as not to bring me help. For there are three kinds of people in the church when persecution comes: some consent, some flee, and some suffer, and it is the part of these that Job plays. "And wild asses rushed upon me in the field": the foolish and untamed, and therefore proud, rush upon me as I confess, that is, upon the church. "And going out to their work": for this is their work, to rush upon me; that is, they have been appointed to this by God. "Bread became sweet to him among the young": he calls persecution sweet bread to the ungodly persecutor, who enjoyed it willingly when he inflicted it on the young. We may take the young either as lovers of pleasure, because they readily give in to such men, or as those who have advanced in the church far enough to have passed beyond the simplicity of childhood, but have not yet reached that manly strength by which even the persecutor is held in contempt. "They have reaped a field not their own before its time": either he is speaking of kinds of persecution, as when they would frighten someone with the loss of a field; or the field is to be understood as the church, which they wanted to reap with persecutions before it was ripe, that is, before the tares had grown up together with it so as to be separated at harvest time. "They will be drenched by the drippings of the mountains": fleeing naked to caves where the rocks drip. "They have snatched the orphan from the breast": orphans and widows are generally to be understood as the people under torment, in the person of the church. "And they have humbled the one who had fallen": one deserted by the help of God or of anyone else; and it is great cruelty not to spare such people. "In straits they have lain in wait unjustly": in times of need. "From the city and from their houses they were cast out": others were cast out by them. "But the soul of the little ones was in great groaning": "was." "Yet God himself has had no care for them": for the ungodly; because by having no care for them now he has made them give up belief in God's judgment, since they did evil with impunity. "And therefore they have been handed over to darkness": the darkness of ignorance of God's judgment. "And suddenly, like a thief": that day will overtake them. "The eye of the adulterer watches for darkness": he wants to show into what darkness the ungodly are handed over through impunity: not the darkness that adulterers and others who do evil by night seek so as not to be recognized by day, but the darkness that lies upon them even in the morning. "He digs through houses in the dark": he mentions other evil deeds. "By day they have sealed themselves up": they have hidden themselves. "They have not known the light, because the shadow of death remains with them all alike": the shadow of death has not left them because the night has withdrawn. "It is light upon the face of the water": compared with earth, those whom the light penetrates are to be understood as brighter, and as an image of lightness; and therefore the shadow of death lies lightly upon them. For they too bear it through the condition of the flesh. Or: he said "It is light upon the face of the water" of those who confess in baptism. "Cursed be their portion upon the earth": may what they have chosen be barren. "For they have snatched from the bosom of orphans": the word, from the heart of the weak, by evil persuasion. "Then his sin was remembered": the sin he thought would be forgotten. "Let every wicked one be broken like an incurable tree": one that does not heal. "For he did no good to the barren woman": the woman who is without the comfort of children. "Rising up, therefore, he does not believe against his own life": he does not believe against his own life; for he ought to have believed that his life was evil, and by that very fact to have risen up. "When he begins to be sick, let him not hope for health": to be sick means to be afflicted. "But he falls into weakness": for the ungodly man seeks in adversity the kind of consolations that make him weaker. "It has withered like a mallow in the heat": his loftiness, because it could not bear the heat of tribulation; and a mallow, because of its weakness. "Or like an ear of grain falling of its own accord from the stalk": because its top was empty; for he himself chose such consolations as would make him weaker still. "Otherwise, who is there to say that I speak falsehood?" If things are otherwise too.

The words of Bildad the Shuhite. "For what is the beginning but fear of him?" This continuation seems to agree with the words in which Job says, "Therefore I shall be troubled at his face; I shall consider and be afraid of him." "Let no one think that the pirates will delay": they tempt without delay, as he permits. "For upon whom will snares not come from him?" That is, when he permits it. By snares he means temptations. "Or how shall a man be righteous before the Lord?" Therefore he justly permits him to be tempted. "Or how shall one born of woman make himself clean?" For unless he is cleansed by God, he is unclean. "If he gives the moon a command, it does not shine": since if the reasons and order of his providence require that the moon should not shine, he will command it not to shine, and it will not shine. But why say this? Does he mean by it that the moon is seen not to be clean before him, because he commands it and it does not shine? Or perhaps the nature of the rational soul is figuratively suggested here, for which the intelligible sun is that true light which enlightens every man. And since the moon shines all the more to earthly eyes the farther it withdraws from the sun, but when it draws near the sun it is extinguished as far as the earth is concerned, let us understand that the soul is divinely commanded to overcome its earthly and mortal birth, by which its splendour appears to those who see with earthly sense, and to appear before wisdom, draw near to it, and be subject to it. Then, rejoicing most secretly in wisdom's light, it will take care not to practise its righteousness before men in order to be seen by them, but when it boasts, it will boast in the Lord; for even when it appears to men, it appears by the gift of the Creator. "Nor are the stars clean before him": in comparison with him.

The words of Job. Whom are you helping, or whom are you going to help? He said this because in his indignation he thought they ought to be punished by God for their injustice. But, speaking to himself, he calls himself back, so as to leave judgment of them to God instead. He does not want to seem to be helping God, or wanting to assist him as though God were too weak to restrain or correct human beings, or giving him advice about what to do with them. Nor does he want to seem to follow him, as though he could grasp why God allows deceitful people to exist and live, when God surpasses every soul that seeks him by a power beyond comprehension. Nor does he want to seem to announce anything to God about them, when a human being has from God even the breath with which he speaks. Shall the giants be reduced to nothing? So it is no wonder if God spares these men, since he does not reduce the giants to nothing. And so that no one could say, "But they were thrust down to the underworld," he added that God sees the underworld. Yet God has placed them where they deserved to be, as he places the righteous, whether now, as they are, or later, as they will be. Still, he never removes them from his sight, for all things are naked before him. So you may take even these proud comforters as neighbours of the giants. Beneath the water, and their neighbours: is "beneath the water" to be understood with "are held" or something of the kind supplied? And there is no covering for destruction: even destruction does not escape him. Stretching out the north over nothing: the north may signify the devil and the earth the sinner, since for both alike hope is empty. Hanging the earth over nothing: in the air. Binding up the water in his clouds: because of the obscurity of prophecy. And the cloud is not torn beneath it: beneath the truth that the cloud held. The cloud is not torn for those who understand the Scriptures, for the Scriptures do not contradict one another, as those who fail to understand them suppose. Who holds back the face of the sun: so that the Sun of righteousness would not be recognized by the ungodly. And spreads his cloud over it: the flesh that the Lord took on. He has set a commandment around, over the face of the water: the peoples. Until the consummation of light: the end of this life, that is, the end of the age. Or it means until those are consummated, that is, made perfect, to whom it was said: For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. The pillars of heaven trembled and were astonished at his rebuke: this happened to Peter through Paul. By his power he calmed the sea: he pacified the world, at whose hands the church was suffering persecution. So the pillars of heaven trembling at his rebuke can also be understood to mean that the strongest members of the church trembled for the weak at the rebuke of the Lord, who permitted the trials of persecution. For a pillar cries out: Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn? And by his prudence the sea monster was wounded: he means that the devil was wounded with pain, because the righteous did not give way to him. And the bars of heaven fear him: either the angels or those who received the keys of the kingdom of heaven. By his command he slew the deserting dragon: he calls the same creature the sea monster. But now he shows how it was wounded: when those who renounced it received the commandment. Behold, these are parts of his way: the way by which one comes to God. But who will know the power of his thunder, when he will make it? By thunder he means the most evident voice of his manifestation, or perhaps the voice he gave through the son of thunder: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. Then the order is: when he will make it, will anyone know the power of his thunder?

And the divine spirit is in my nostrils: this shows that he speaks prophetically and knows by prophecy that these comforters of his are full of deceit. Far be it from me to call you righteous until I die: even if you persecute me to death because I rebuke you freely. For I will not set aside the innocent: nor you, however [?]. For I am not conscious of having done anything wicked: those who fear that something true may be charged against them usually spare others. For what hope does the ungodly have? That he waits. So that no one would think he had wished evil on his enemies, he showed here in what spirit he had spoken. He wants their ungodliness to be overthrown and their pride to perish. This happens when the soul that was held guilty is set free from ungodliness, and it is set free through the confession of the penitent and the grace of the God who pardons. So: For what hope does the ungodly have? This is a question and its answer: That he waits and trusts in the Lord, in case he may be set free, or the Lord may hear his prayers. Another sense could indeed be found in these words, namely that it is all said out of despair and the ungodly have no hope at all. But that sense does not fit either the book or the faith, since against it Scripture says: But to one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness. Therefore what follows is understood to speak of the Lord's grace. Or if necessity comes upon him: this is why we must wait for the grace of the one who sets us free. For in his necessity, that is, in his temptation, did he have confidence in his merits in God's sight? Or if he calls, will God hear him? Not if he calls as though trusting in his own works, which are nothing. Therefore I will declare to you what is in the hand of the Lord: what God has arranged. Behold, you all know that you speak vain things in vain: this is why grace must now be awaited. For how could he plead the merits of his works while speaking vain things in vain? But the possession of the mighty will come upon them from the Almighty: so that the mighty, that is, the devil and his angels, will possess them. He calls them mighty because these men will grow weak by following vanity, so that those leaders and princes of vanity will prevail over them. In the same way the Lord calls the devil strong for no other reason than that he holds the weak in his grip. If his sons are many, they will be for slaughter: by his sons he means those who invite him, the persuader of false doctrines, to lead them astray into damnation. And if they grow into young men, they will be in want; that is, if they are confirmed in error, they will be in want, for vanity has not satisfied them. And those around him will die by death: those most like him in leading others astray. And he will have no pity on their widows: the peoples whom he led astray along with them, left desolate by the death of their husbands, as though he had kept faith with them like a husband in his promise of error. And if he gathers silver like earth: that is, if the prudent and the wise agree with them while they are still earth and mud, that is, while they still think foolish and carnal thoughts, then afterwards, corrected and coming to know the truth, they will turn to the righteous. For their houses will be like the moth and the spider, which he kept: the heart or the conscience. Or by houses he meant the defences with which they protect themselves. These are cunning and full of hiding places, but very weak, like the little case in which the moth hides and the spider's hollow, into which it withdraws, covering and shutting itself in. "Which he kept" is understood to mean that the spider kept itself in that hollow, since not all spiders do this. The image refers to the voluntary, inward corruption of wicked thought, and to the useless works that the ungodly man has, as it were, carefully kept for himself in his house. The rich man will sleep and will not add: because after death he will add no riches to those very impieties. He opened his eyes, and he is not: for in the resurrection he will not find himself rich, as he had supposed. The surge will carry him off, and he will go away: either the surge of the sea, which is the tribulation of the world, or the heat that dries up plants that have no root. And it will winnow him from his place: either from his hope, or God will winnow him from his place, so that he is not in God's place, that is, among the people in whom God has dwelt. And he will hurl upon him and will not spare: a heap of punishments, as it were. He will clap his hands over him. As it is said: And I will laugh over your destruction. For he will not mourn over the destruction of the ungodly.

For there is a place for silver, from which it comes: the prudent, who are more given to action. And a place for gold, where it is refined: the wise, who are given to contemplation. For iron comes from the earth: these metals are all to be taken in a good sense without distinction. He mentioned iron for this reason, that it makes no difference, as if he had been speaking of iron above as well, although the strong could be understood by iron. For in truth there is no distinction in wisdom among the people who are in it [?]. And bronze, like stones, is hewn out: because all of it is separated from the earth. This shows that the good are mixed with the wicked for a time precisely because the good are separated out from the wicked and refined through them. They are like metals needed for a work or a building: they have to be smelted out of the earth itself and shaped, and so must be separated from it. After this separation the earth may have its own place and order, as the ungodly have theirs through condemnation according to their deserts. And he himself found every end: to what end he would bring each thing. By "found" he meant "established." Stone, darkness and the shadow of death: the stone, that is, the Old Testament, was given to darkness and the shadow of death, that is, to those who pursue carnal things, even though they expected these things from the one God. There in their pride they did not cut through the torrent; that is, they did not pass through the flowing away of temporal things to something solid, but were swept along by that very flow. And the torrent was cut off from the ash: that is, by one who confesses his sins and does not boast of the merits of his works, which came about through the grace of the New Testament. The cutting of the torrent from the ash: from men. And they were moved away by men: by flatterers, while God did not rebuke them, towards the very things that had been promised them, so losing their primacy [?]. Earth from which bread came forth: supply "I mean those very people who were moved," from whom, as from earth, the bread of the Lord came forth. And he will burn it: the unbelieving earth, by the heavenly judgment of the Lord. A place of sapphire, its stones. The order is: a place of sapphire, that is, of what is precious and necessary for building the heavenly city. And heaps of gold for it: it has not a little gold, but heaps. A path that the bird did not know: the humility of the Lord. Nor has the vulture's eye seen it: the devil's. The lion has not passed over it: one proud in his strength. He stretched out his hand on the hardest stone: for God is able to raise up children to Abraham from stones. And he broke through the banks of the rivers: to water the whole. By rivers he meant the preachers of the word. They wanted to be kept within their banks, so as to preach wholly to the circumcision. But my eye has seen every precious thing: the human eye, through the Word made flesh. He revealed the depths of the rivers: the strength to endure persecution in martyrdom lies hidden and deep within a person until it is revealed by the trial of persecution. And he showed his power in the light: in those to whom he said, You are the light of the world. Through them, too, no small part of the Jews was converted. The abyss said, It is not in me: so people placed in the abyss could not find wisdom, because it is not there. Enclosed gold will not be given for it: that is, treasure. It will not be inferior to the gold of Ophir: as if he were saying, "Seek it even so, if indeed it is not inferior to the gold of Ophir." Gold and glass will not equal it: either some beautiful glass is meant, or else it is because there are people who love glass more than wisdom. And vessels of gold are its exchange: supply "are not." And lofty things and gabis will not be remembered: they will be forgotten in comparison with it. Or else "lofty things and gabis" stand for everything proud: let them not be remembered, so that through humility you may draw wisdom out of its hidden places. Where was wisdom found? He says that man could not find it except through grace, and that therefore the heart must turn to God. It is hidden from the eyes of every man: because it does not belong to the senseless [?]. Destruction and death said: the lost and the dead, when they live in pleasures. The Lord commended its way: humility, which is hidden from the birds of the sky. And he himself knows its place: what is the place of wisdom but the Father? For when it is said, I am in him and he is in me, they are, as it were, places for each other. For he looks upon everything that is under heaven: he knows things in the way he made them, and not by the senses. The weights and measures of the winds: the whole creation is signified by a part. And rightly it is said that all things were made in weight, measure and number, for in them the Creator is understood. When he made them, as he saw, he numbered them: he did not look outside himself in order to make them, but within himself, like a craftsman. And the way of the storms with voices: "of storms" is put for "of temptations," and "of temptations" for those who are tempted, as one might speak of the voices of a shipwreck meaning the voices of the shipwrecked. Then he saw it and set it forth: in predestination the Lord saw the way by which the tempted would turn back. He prepared it and searched it out: in predestination, not in action.

Who will restore me to the months of former days? These words seem to be spoken in the person of the church together with Christ its head, as if the whole man himself were speaking at a time when tribulations and temptations abound. It is as in the days of which the Lord says: Days will come when you will long to see one of these days, and you will not see it. For at the time when the Lord was on earth there was no anxiety, even though the Christian people was still small. It consisted of those who had believed in him, among them the more than five hundred brothers to whom he also deigned to appear after the resurrection, as the apostle says. So at that time there was no anxiety that the church might be badly governed by bad men or torn apart by the snares of heresies or schisms. It did not even suffer bodily persecution; it endured no adversity, whether from within or from without. So Job speaks in the person of the man, that is, of the people belonging to the New Testament, longing for those days, as the Lord had foretold. And perhaps he called them months rather than years because from the time the Lord chose his disciples until his passion there were not years but months. When his lamp shone over my head: either the Lord's flesh, visibly present, or the word from the mouth of one bodily present. When the word of the Lord watched over my house: so that I diligently guarded my way of life. And my servants were around me: those who obeyed humbly, ministering what was needed. When butter rained along my ways: along my conduct, the exultation of faith and of good works. When my mountains abounded with milk: when the prophets were well explained to the little ones. When I went out early in the morning into the city: either when brightness was already dawning after the darkness of fear had passed, or at the beginning of the church, when it was neither fully hidden nor fully manifest. And a seat was set for me in the streets: the crowds conferred on me the authority to teach. When the young men saw me, they hid: those given over to lusts. But the old men rose: the prudent. And the mighty ceased speaking: those proud of their own doctrines. For the ear heard and called me blessed: a people I did not know served me; as soon as they heard me, they obeyed me. And the eye that saw me turned aside: the eye of the Jews who did not believe. And the mouth of the widow blessed me: the mouth of the soul that has renounced marriage to the devil. Behold, a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow. And I clothed myself with judgment as with a cloak: in preferring spiritual things to carnal ones. Do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, that is, with what intention it acts. For in wearing a cloak the left hand is covered while the right is left free. This is what someone does who rightly judges to what end his actions should be directed. I searched out the judgment I did not know: Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what will we have? He says it was part of his happiness that he had someone he could ask about the judgment to come. I broke the millstones of the wicked: so that they would no longer devour the people as if they were bread. My age will grow old, and like the palm tree I shall live a long time: it will be prolonged, and I shall be like the palm tree in everlasting honour, loftiness and uprightness. And dew will linger on my harvest: a field is called a harvest from the time it is sown and begins to sprout. My glory is new with me: that is, the glory of the New Testament. And my bow will advance in my hand: I will do what I command. And they added nothing to my speech: this signifies the perfection of the gospel, for the speech given to the synagogue needed something added. But they rejoiced when I spoke to them: because the earlier speech brought fear, the later one love. And if I laughed at them, they did not believe: this concerns the things he spoke in parables in such a way that they were not understood. Yet he was not thought to be saying vain things, as the words seemed to sound. This is the laughter of Sarah, which signified that they did everything in prophecy: hence those who say something figuratively [?]. I chose their way and sat as chief: either by taking on mortality or by eating with tax collectors and sinners, but in such a way that I was their chief, leading them to salvation. And I dwelt like a king girded with the strong: those who left their own and followed him. As one who comforts the sorrowful: he means those who rejoiced in hope while they were sorrowful over the present life. As it was said, Blessed are those who mourn, and: as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing. These are people who cannot reach the greatness of which it was said: But whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.

But now the lowliest mock me, now those younger in time admonish me: because such people were also born later in the church and do not make much progress. He said "admonish me" because through ecclesiastical offices they receive the power of preaching to the people things which they themselves do not do. Whose fathers I despised: he said "their fathers," meaning those whose sons they are by imitation, to whom it was said at that time: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites. And the strength of their hands was as nothing to me: the power of the fathers, who at that time were so very powerful that they crucified the Lord. In them all life perished: because they did not correct themselves even at the end. Unstable from want and hunger: insatiable from various desires. Who fled into the desert yesterday: taking refuge in the law as an excuse, though they did not understand it plainly; and because they had received the law in the desert, he says "fleeing into the desert yesterday." For as "today" belongs to the New Testament, so "yesterday" belongs to the Old; for of the New it was said: Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, and: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Who gnawed the bark of trees: because they took as food the figures of the law, by which useful things were covered. Whose food was the root of plants: the sacraments which they had been commanded to celebrate bodily, as things clinging to the earth; yet from them the fruit of a pure understanding was to rise and be carried above the earth into freedom, where they could not reach. Without honor and cast off and lacking every good: having lost the honor of primacy, and fallen from the hope of the promise; because they had lost even the earthly gift itself, as they deserved, and they do not hold the kingdom of heaven. Who ate the roots of trees because of great hunger: what was said of the roots of plants with reference to the fruit of grain is to be understood of the roots of trees with reference to the fruit of wine and oil. For the church has received all these spiritual fruits, whose roots, entangled in the earth, were the sacraments which the Jews were compelled to observe bodily: the sabbath, circumcision, sacrifices, and the other roots of this kind that bore spiritual foods. Thieves rose up against me: those who by dark deceits attained honors not due to them, honors that properly belong to the righteous. Whose houses were caves in the rocks: those who defended their lusts and covered them with certain obscurities of the divine books. And they cried out among the trees: their sins were manifest, though they tried to cover them with the obscurity of the scriptures as if with the shade of trees. Hence: The cry of Sodom has gone up to me. And in many places scripture puts "cry" for manifest sins: so that whatever is conceived in the heart is a word, and becomes a cry when it proceeds into deed. Who dwelt beneath the stocks of the earth: they can be understood to dwell not even in the stocks, where those are who at least keep the precepts carnally, but even below the stocks. For stocks are not yet the fruits themselves, but that from which the fruit-bearing parts of trees or plants rise; provided, however, that the plant is of a fruit-bearing kind, since plants of a non-fruit-bearing kind are also said to have stocks. Sons of fools and of base men: of the Jews; for above he called these their fathers on account of imitation, because these too walk under the name of God, whom they do not worship. He calls the Jews fools and base, who on the contrary were confident not only that they were guides of the blind but also that they were sons of Abraham, and boasted that with him as father they were noble. But when they hear: They are blind guides of the blind, they are shown to be fools; and when they hear: If you are sons of Abraham, do the works of Abraham, they are shown to be base by their degeneracy. Their name and honor extinguished from the earth: for it existed, but has been extinguished. But now I am their lyre: theirs, I mean, whose fathers those men are; they had me for the ear, not for the heart. And they hold me as a tale: an empty and useless telling and hearing, even though they both tell of me and hear me. They abhorred me, going far away: having become far from righteousness by sinning, and by cursing the precepts of righteousness with their wicked conduct. Nor did they refrain from spitting in my face: for the face of Christ is detestable to those who shudder with contempt at his precepts; or: they made me known in a bad light by the depravity of their conduct. For opening his quiver he afflicted me: the hidden things from which temptations arise. And they put a bridle on my face: so that I would consent to them against my will, carrying them while they led me where they wished, down into their own depths. And sprouting on the right they rose up: they did indeed spring up, by showing favor and giving good admonitions, in order to satisfy their own desires, not by persecuting. They bound my feet with fetters: the fetters of ecclesiastical duties, so that my feet could not flee from them. My paths were broken up: so that the paths by which the good are accustomed to walk, seeking not their own things but the things of Christ, could no longer be seen. For he stripped me of my robe: of my former authority, to which people usually yield; this happens when the multitude and the habit of sinners prevail. And he wounded me with his darts: with the precepts, by which I see evils and am tormented because I cannot restrain them. He abused me as he willed: God used even my calamity and misery for his righteousness, as he willed. I am wrapped in sorrows: I suffer both in myself and in others; fightings without, fears within. Who is weak, and I am not weak? And my sorrows are renewed; my hope departs like the wind: those who have turned to hope in temporal things regard what I promise as something empty. And my salvation has passed away like a cloud: they do not hope for the promised salvation, because of their love for present well-being. And now my soul will be poured out upon me: by sinning. By night my bones were broken: he says that the firmness he had was snatched from him. And my sinews were loosened: my past actions. With great power he seized my robe: to show his power, now by afflicting and afterward by restoring. And he encompassed me like the hem of my garment: he left me only a little authority. My portion is in earth and ashes: in penitence, because it is the lowest state. They stood and considered me: and while I lay prostrate the proud stood, looking for something in me to censure. And you have cast me away from salvation: he grieves for those who have lost the hope of restoration. For the earth is the house of every mortal: he says he fears death because his way of life is not in heaven, as is true of the many in the church who are wicked and live in an earthly way. And would that I could kill myself: so as to die to the world. Or ask another to do this for me: either a better angel, or God, through whom I might be corrected. I awaited good things: he grieves because these things befell him suddenly. My belly has boiled up and will not be silent: the inward parts, or the memory, by which the church recalls what she was at first and how she has been afflicted with groanings. And I stood in the assembly crying out: because she was not heard in the throng of those who would not correct themselves. My skin has grown very black: from the things she suffered from without. My lyre has been turned to mourning: the good works with which she used to praise God joyfully.

I made a covenant with my eyes: have I begun to hope for visible things? That I should not think about a virgin: here "far be it" is to be understood. From this point he now begins to recount the merits of the church in those who persevere to the end amid great temptations, when iniquity abounds and the love of many grows cold. And I will not think about a virgin: about the incorruption of wisdom or of righteousness. And what other portion is there from God above? "I will not think" is understood. Or thus: and what is there, if not that? If I have walked with mockers: it is now hard for the good who are in the church not to be associated with such people. Or if my foot has hastened to deceit: hypocrisy. Let me sow, and let others eat my fruits: as happened to the Jews, that is, to say things that others do rather than they themselves. Let me be without root upon the earth: so that I may easily wither. For the one who does what he says stands firm on the earth as on a rock. If my heart has followed a woman: so as to seek its own glory among the people of God rather than God's glory, which is rightly due to him alone. Or if I have laid siege to her doors: if I have craftily played upon the desires or the fear of that people, by which they might be driven to serve me rather than God. Then let my wife also please another: let my reputation please the devil; for when we please him, we displease God, since he rejoices in our evils. And let my sons be humbled: my deeds, or my imitators. For the fury of my soul is untamed to defile another man's wife: by claiming her for myself. And if I have despised the cause of my manservant or my maidservant when they were judged before me: in accordance with what was said: If, then, you have worldly cases. By servants he meant lay people still given over to worldly affairs. And if he makes a visitation, what answer shall I give? In tribulation what kind of conscience do I have, since I despised these things? Were not they too conceived in the womb, as I was? For the same things are preached to all in the sacraments; they believe the same things. And we were alike in the womb. For the one does not renounce the world in any other way than the one who is to serve God fully. And from my mother's womb I was their guide: for the church does this from her very beginning. Or if I have despised the naked man perishing and did not clothe him: if, by faith in the forgiveness of sins, I did not cover from the nakedness of foulness—that is, of sin—one who was perishing as if without a tunic; for he now despairs because of the multitude of his sins. And hence: and whose sins are covered. If the shoulders of the weak have not blessed me: covered from above with the hope of immortality as with a cloak. But lest after faith in the forgiveness of sins they should think it enough to be free of fear of the punishment of past sins and begin to hope for temporal things, he aptly added: they were warmed by the fleece of my sheep, because they were rescued from the cold of earthly hope by considering those sheep, if through renunciation they laid aside carnal things following the example of the shorn flock. If I have lifted my hand against the orphan: who, not finding a father, might follow a creature or a man. Trusting that I have much help: wishing to lord it over them. Let my shoulder part from my neck: this happens to those who separate themselves from the church in their wish to lord it over peoples, so that they suffer severance as the penalty of severance. By the shoulder or the arm, actions are signified. For fear restrained me: lest I lift my hand against the orphan. And I shall not bear up under its weight: if I should want to oppress the orphan. If I made gold my strength: did I presume upon doctrine or upon the wisdom of God? And if I trusted in precious stone: as if in my own works. If I rejoiced when my wealth was great: as though over what was my own; rather, let him who boasts boast in the Lord. If I set my soul on countless things—with all of these is to be understood: let my arm fall from my shoulder—: that I should be loved by many. And my heart was secretly deceived. The order is: if I set my soul on countless things and my heart was secretly deceived: that is, if I consented to such a thought as to presume upon myself. And if I kissed my hand, putting it to my mouth: if I rejoiced as if over my own works. And if I rejoiced at the ruin of my enemy: an enemy of the church, as the persecutors of the church are. Let my ear hear my curse: let it be brought home to my awareness. Let me be a reproach among my people, defamed: before the people of the saints, so that he may be separated as one mocked. And if my maidservants often said: flatterers. Who will grant that we be filled with his flesh? Since I was very good: so that they might imitate carnal happiness in me. Yet I did not do these things; for, so that they would not say this, I did not show myself good in such matters. The stranger did not lodge outside: I received the one who was a stranger in the world. And if, sinning willfully, I hid my sin: for if we sin willfully after we have received the knowledge of the truth. Or if I let the weak man go out of my door with an empty lap: so that he went out of the door precisely because his lap was empty. Who will grant me a hearer? Who will grant me to be heard? If I did not fear the hand of the Lord, with which he wrote: If you do not forgive, neither will your Father forgive you. If I have any written bond. The order is: if I have any written bond, and did not tear it up upon my shoulders, then, crowned, I shall read it publicly. Lifting it upon my shoulders and crowned, I shall read it publicly: that is, against my own face—"I will set you before your face"—because I shall be put to shame before the crowd of the people, since I did not do the Lord's command, which I had already said I had done, first denying that I had any written bond, which is afterward brought against me. If ever the land groaned against me: the tenants of the church, because I am wicked. Or its furrows wept together: in which seeds are received and from which fruits are given; "together" because I am both wicked myself and was sowing wicked seeds. Or if I ate its strength alone, without payment: the very mercy by which the one being taught shares with the one who teaches him; "alone" means not repaying the one who gave. Or if by deceit I grieved the soul of the lord of the land: not showing myself worthy of the passion of him who poured out his soul for me. Do not grieve the Holy Spirit in you. Instead of wheat let nettles spring up for me: instead of spiritual teachers, teachers for itching ears, through the wranglings of men corrupt in mind and bereft of the truth. And thorns instead of barley: instead of carnal people who obey, sinners and those who resist. For Job was righteous in his own sight: in his own conscience.

The words of Elihu the Buzite. God has cast him off, not man: so that I may give this as the reason why they kept silent. And I will not answer him with your words: for I shall say such things that he cannot answer me as he answered us. Since, then, I waited and they did not speak: he says this as if turning to Job. My belly is like a wineskin full of new wine: scripture commends him, because he is about to speak in prophecy. And like a smith's bellows burst: I speak forcefully to break down hardness; that is also why he is said to be angry. For there would be no need for me to speak if you had answered him. Otherwise moths will devour me too: either like you, or like all who are awed by persons.

My heart is pure in words: not double. The divine spirit who made me: understand "is," so that it reads: It is the divine spirit who made me. How then do you say: I am righteous, and he has not heard me? As if Job had said this to an adversary. For the Lord speaks once: as if the Lord made the call of all the righteous once, and divine providence carries it out in time with each individual. Through a dream or in a visitation by night: either in ignorance or in tribulation. Or as when fierce fear falls upon men while they sleep in their chambers: free of care. And may he rescue his body from ruin: figuratively, like "bones." And he spared his soul from death: when he has converted him, he will spare him. Because war will come, and again he will rebuke him in sickness on his bed: after conversion he now tests him, so that he may not presume upon himself. And the multitude of his bones has wasted away: his confidence in himself. And he will not be able to take any food: consolation from temporal things. And he will renew his body like plaster on a wall: a change of life; here too it is figurative, with reference to a building, that is, being built into fellowship. And he will soften his flesh like a little child's: so that he may not be hard with pride; according to how Elihu sees it, Job, now humble, is tested through renewal. And he entered with a cheerful face, with confession: ready for temptations. Save my soul, lest I come to corruption: here is the temptation of death. Three times with a man: of conversion, of testing, of death. But he rescued my soul from death: because this trial, that of death, still remains. That my soul may praise him in the light: so then prayers will cease, since there will be no need.

Then Elihu answered and said: as one says, "and he went on." And you who have knowledge, give ear: with spiritual ears. For the ear tests words: this one, the carnal ear. What good is it that Job said: I am righteous? What good did he say by saying it? And in my judgment he has lied. Hence: I awaited good things; so "he has lied" refers to what turned out contrary to his hope. Who is a man like Job? These are still Job's words; for he said: He who walks with God will not be visited: here he thinks Job was deceived, because he did all those things in this hope; or at least: that Job thinks that one who walks with the Lord is not visited for good. Far be impiety from the Lord: either that he should not visit for good one who has walked with him, or that, even if he visits him in temptation, he should act impiously and unjustly. He is impious who says to a king: You act unjustly. But you ought not to say it, since you are not impious. Rightly it says "who says," not "who has said," lest he be impious on that account already; as one says "it is done" of [?] the one who does this. To princes, "most impiously": as if he were saying to angels—except Michael, your prince—"you act most impiously"; or: if it is so impious to say this to princes, how much more to a king! For they wickedly abused it when, being weak, they were shut out: they made bad use of their exclusion, when on account of their weakness they were shut out from that vision by which all things are seen to be ordered and governed by God in the most orderly way. They made bad use of it in this, that they preferred to follow their own spirit, thinking that God does not care about these things; for from this it will come about for them, in vain, that in their needs they cry out and beg a man when they ought to have begged God. Nor will there be a place—and there is no shadow of death—where those who do wicked things may hide. The shadow of death is not there for this purpose, that they may hide; as in: It is not the old who have wisdom, because old age is not the cause of wisdom; and: Do not greet a heretic, that is, not on the ground that he is a heretic. And he will overturn the night, and they will be humbled: so that what was beneath them is above them, that is, so that what was subject to them may press down upon them. And he extinguished the impious: they seemed to themselves to shine. And they did not know his righteous judgments: he says what good God has made from their iniquity: that the cry of the poor is carried to him. He himself will give rest, and who will be able to condemn? Not the kind of rest that men seek, which is disturbed by those tribulations; if God justifies, who is there to condemn? <Against a nation> and against a man alike: against Gentiles and Jews. Who makes a hypocrite reign because of the perversity of the people. To him it is said: You, then, who teach another, do you not teach yourself? Apart from me I shall see; you show me: in rebuking you, do I perhaps fail to see that I myself deserve rebuke? This is to be read as a question. If I have done iniquity, I will not do so again: having been corrected by you. Does he require it of you because you rejected it? That is, because you rebuked. And a wise man will hear my word: that God cares for all things. But Job has not spoken in wisdom: in thinking that something unjust has befallen him from God.

Why did you think this in judgment? Why did you judge this? Who are you, who said: I am righteous in the sight of the Lord? In the sight of the Lord you said: I am righteous. Both things are blameworthy in a man. The first is if it is said proudly, or if it is false that he is righteous even by the standard of human righteousness. The second is that a man can never truly say that he is righteous in the sight of God, for compared with God anyone at all is unrighteous. Or you say: What does it profit you, or what shall I do, if I have sinned? For it seems to him that Job said this to God as if, on the one hand, his sin profits God, so that by this pain he is driven to piety; this is where he says: Do not teach me to be ungodly; or is it good for you if I act unjustly? Or, on the other hand, as if he harms God by sinning, and so God pursues him in this way, pressing hard on him as on his enemy, so as not to suffer some harm from him. For he had also said this: If I have sinned, what can I do to you? So Elihu answered both points in the words that follow: I will give an answer to you and to my three friends. Look up to heaven and see; consider the clouds, how high they are above you. If you have sinned, what do you accomplish? He confirms what Job had said: If I have sinned, what can I do to you? Or if you have done many unjust things, what will you be able to do? "You have done many unjust things" says more than what he said above, "you have sinned." But still, what will you be able to do to God, when you cannot even harm the clouds? And if you are righteous, what will you give him? Conversely: just as your righteousness does him no good, so your unrighteousness does him no harm. Or what will he receive from your hand? That is, even if you wished to give. This is said on account of sacrifices, which fools think God takes as though he needed them. Your ungodliness is for a man like you, and your righteousness for a son of man: it is to them that the one does harm or the other does good. But with these verses he confirmed rather than refuted the opinion Job expressed: If I have sinned, what can I do to you? So it follows that he must show why in this life men are afflicted by the wrongs done by the wicked, among whom the devil with his angels is also counted, the prince of all wrongs and iniquities. For since sinners cannot harm God, why does he hand them over to the power of the wicked to be afflicted? And he explains this next, saying: Because of the multitude they will cry out; they will shout because of the arm of many. And he did not say: Where is God who made me? For they suffer these things so that they may seek God, not so that they may shout in vain. His saying "made me" serves as proof that he who made a man will not abandon him when he seeks him. Who appoints the night watches: that is, the times of this age, ordered under fixed powers, because he who made man will not leave him without a guard even in this night of error. Who separates me from the four-footed beasts of the earth and has made me wiser than the birds of the sky: for this is how the Lord is to be sought in the afflictions of this life, that we do not desire earthly goods from him, since we are already better than the beasts before we receive them. There they will cry out, and you will not hear. By "there" he meant in the multitude, in the affliction of those who cry out because of the arm of many; or else "there" means "for this reason," as in: There those who work iniquity have fallen. And "you will not hear": he said this of him. From the wrongs done by the wicked: "they will cry out" is to be understood. For the Lord does not wish to look upon vain things: he does not wish to come to the aid of those who ask for vain things, who do not cry out in affliction in order to obtain everlasting goods, though it was for this very purpose that they were separated from the beasts of the earth and made wiser than the birds of the sky. Instead they cry out because they are not prosperous in the iniquity of this age. For the Almighty himself looks upon those who do righteousness, and he will save me: just as he who looks into the inmost heart sees those who do it, so he saves them with that salvation which he himself sees in secret, for eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him. Therefore, even if man's vain wellbeing is disturbed, the Father who sees in secret nevertheless gives help in tribulation. Be judged before him, then, if you can praise him as he is; for Job seemed to be saying this when he said: Would that there were an arbiter for us! And now, because he does not visit his wrath, nor has he taken severe note of offenses: that is, taken note of them for punishment. Hence the verse: For I acknowledge my iniquity; and in the same place: Turn your face away from my sins. So he has taken note of offenses; that is why men suffer tribulation in this age, but not severely, because by correcting in part you give room for repentance. And Job opened his mouth in vain; in his ignorance he multiplies words.

Bear with me a little, that I may teach you; for I still have words within me. Taking up my knowledge from afar: since as long as we are in this body we are away from the Lord. But by my works I will speak what is just. This is so that it may not be said to him what God says to the sinner: Why do you recount my righteous acts and take my covenant in your mouth? But you have hated instruction. So here one must speak by works; for knowledge is taken up from afar, in part and in a riddle. But when what is perfect comes, what is in part will be taken away, and it will no longer be from afar, for we shall see him as he is. In truth, and you will understand unjustly words that are not unjust: he says that the very things Job was suffering are words of God, spoken in truth and not unjust; but he thinks that Job understands them unjustly, since [?] Job supposes he can complain that he suffers undeservedly, whereas it has been said even of the tribulation of the righteous: It is time for judgment to begin at the house of the Lord. And know that the Lord will not cast off the innocent: although he chastens whom he loves and scourges every son whom he receives. Mighty in strength of heart, he does not give life to the ungodly: although he seems to spare him for a time. And "mighty in strength of heart" is well said, because he will not give him life at the time when the ungodly man seeks room for a late repentance with tears and will not find it. Nor will he bend to mercy the one who then judges mightily, whom he now despises while he mercifully admonishes. And he will grant judgment to the poor: by which he will judge those at whose hands they suffer iniquity. And "of the poor" is well said, so that by "the ungodly" above you understand the rich man, that is, the proud. He will not take his eyes away from the righteous: even when he tests him as in a furnace by the trial of tribulation, he will not take from him the understanding by which God is known and worshiped. By this he shows clearly enough that the punishment of the ungodly is blindness itself, even when they seem to be spared. And with kings on the throne: "he made them sit" is understood, that is, the righteous. And he calls kings those who rule their flesh. Hence that saying: What king, going out to wage war against another king, and so on. And he made them sit forever, and they will be exalted: here too what he said above, "with kings on the throne," is understood. He said "they will be exalted" because they were humbled. And those who are fettered with fetters: the bond from which the apostle says it is good for him to be released and to be with Christ, that is, the ties of this life, in which the corruptible body weighs down the soul. They will be caught in the cords of poverty: they will be bound by long habits of carnal delights, which arise from the want of those things by which mortal life is sustained and carried on. And their works are announced to them: certainly not good works. Either they are those very impulses of desire of which it is said: I know that good does not dwell in my flesh; and even if these do not reign in our mortal body so that we obey them, they are nevertheless present. Or they are the works by which man deserved to come to these things through the inheritance of sin. And their offenses, when they have been strengthened: these are the very works he spoke of above. For they cannot easily be announced, that is, made manifest, to the weak, but only to those who have already advanced so far as to have passed beyond all that iniquity which is commonly recognized in the most open deeds of shame and crime. But he will hear the righteous: namely the one who lives by faith, so that he ascribes to God's grace and not to his own merits not only that he has been justified according to the measure of this life, but also what remains, that he be freed from the whole evil of offenses. These are the things that the truth announces to the faithful when they have been strengthened, when they are caught in the cords of poverty; for they are still fettered with fetters, not yet exalted to sit on the throne with kings forever. And he said that they will turn from iniquity. With "and he said," "God" is to be understood. If they obey and serve, they will complete their days in good things and their years in glory: then indeed there will be no sin in man, because there will be no strife of death, that is, the want that belongs to mortality, which came about through sin, when at last it will be said: Where, O death, is your strife? But he will not save the ungodly, because they would not know the Lord: this seems to apply rather to the Gentiles. And when they were admonished, they were disobedient: this applies to the Jews and to all who resemble them through disobedience, even within the church. And the hypocrites in heart will lay up fury: the fury with which they crucified the Lord. They will not cry out, because he has bound them: by the honor of the name above all nations. Let their soul therefore die in youth: in the pride with which they exalted themselves as though on the merits of their works. And let their life be wounded by angels: this is more fittingly taken as "by messengers of the truth," who are to some a fragrance of life unto life, to others a fragrance of death unto death. Because they afflicted the weak and powerless one: that weakness of God which is stronger than men. But he will establish the judgment of the meek: the Lord himself, by the example of his meekness, defers even the vengeance due to those who imitate him, yet it will surely come. And because the abyss beguiled you away from the mouth of the enemy: the depth of this age, as it seemed to his persecutors, beguiled Christ away from the mouth of the false witness; for he turns his speech to the Lord himself. Poured out beneath it: "the darts deceived" [?] is to be understood; for those weighed down with earthly desires are said to be poured out beneath the abyss. And your table came down full of fatness: the sacrament of his body and blood, the bread that came down from heaven. Judgment will not fail the righteous: although the poor eat and are filled so as to imitate the sufferings of the Lord, made ready by the fullness of love, he does not for that reason fail to carry out judgment for them speedily. And wrath will be upon the ungodly because of the ungodliness of the gifts they received for their iniquities: he calls gifts all temporal advantages whatever, for the sake of which iniquities are committed. Let not the will of your mind turn you aside: this is said to the Lord, not with the authority of one who admonishes or the boldness of one who commands, but in the language of prophecy, which foretells the future through the imperative mood, as in: Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one. From the prayers of the weak, when they are in need: those who cry out, Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death? And all who have strength: those who presume on their own works and wish to establish their own righteousness. Do not draw them out by night: let it be manifest that you are separating them from the people, whether those proud ones who were broken off from the olive tree, or the branches cut off from the vine, from which heresies and schisms have arisen. So that peoples may go up in their place: so that the weak things of this world may be grafted in when the strong are put to shame, for whoever humbles himself will be exalted, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled. But take care that you do nothing unseemly: lest the name of the Lord God and his doctrine be blasphemed, when people say (people whose condemnation is just): Let us do evil that good may come. For this you have chosen over poverty: you have chosen not only the poverty of one who confesses, but beyond it the beauty of life and conduct, so that the saving doctrine may be adorned in all things. Behold, God will console, or: will be strengthened in his strength: because though he was crucified in weakness, yet he lives by the power of God. For who is mighty like him? Or who is there to examine his works? That is, as though judging him, when he himself is the judge of the living and the dead. Or who is there to say: He has acted unjustly? Remember that his works are great, which men have praised: the evangelists and all preachers of the word whose life agrees with their ministry. Every man looks to him: mindful of human weakness. All men who are pricked to the heart: it is through repentance for their sins that they are men. Behold, God is great, and we shall not know: "great," because where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more; "we shall not know" is said in the person of those upon whom blindness has come in part, until the fullness of the Gentiles should come in. The number of his years is infinite: this is set down on account of his eternity. And to him the drops of rain are countless: for this, that the gospel has filled men who are preachers, can be counted until the end of the age, until the knowledge that is in part is taken away and what is perfect comes, face to face. The rain will pour out along its paths: for the ways of the wicked will not receive it. The clouds will flow and grow dark over very many men: because even if the gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. He has set an hour for the beasts, and they know the order of their lair: for the ox has known its owner and the donkey its master's manger. At all these things his mind is not astonished: the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. Nor is your heart changed from the body: so that, lifted up from the earth, it may be held on high toward the Lord. If he should think to spread out the mist: so that those who see may become blind. Just like a tent he spreads it out: for dwelling in mortal flesh as in a tent, he was not recognized through it by his persecutors, while he yielded to them and stretched it out and spread it on the cross. Behold, he pours out his light over all things: the light he had hidden when blindness came in part upon Israel, he pours out over all nations. And he covered the roots of the sea: he rebuked the greed of the world. For the light covers not in order to hide but in order to make manifest. For by them he judged the peoples, showing them their sins by the light of truth. He will give food to very many: namely to those who acknowledge their sins when they are rebuked, and who hunger and thirst for righteousness. In the hands he covered the light: if the word comes from "inmanes" (the cruel), this refers to those who do not forgive men their sins, though they wish to be forgiven by God; but if from "manus" (hands), it refers to those who are puffed up because of their hands, that is, their works, and justify themselves. He said "he covered the light" meaning so that it may not be seen by them, because their foolish heart was darkened. And he gave command concerning it to the contrary: so that those who do the truth, whether by forgiving so that they may be forgiven, or by confessing their evils so that they submit themselves to God's grace, may themselves come to the light, that their works may be made manifest, because they have been wrought in God and not in themselves. For the merciful man is the contrary of the cruel, and the humble of the proud. That he might announce concerning it to his friend: concerning that light, that is, concerning what he covered in order to hide it from the cruel and ungrateful, so that he might announce it, that is, disclose it, no longer to a slave under the law but to one reconciled through grace. Or "to his friend" means to his imitator, because the Son of Man too came not to be served but to serve. A possession against him, those who strive to ascend: so that those who draw themselves out of earthly things may possess that very light. For it is announced to those who are still striving to ascend, because when they have ascended there will be no need of anyone to announce it to those who see face to face. But "against him," said of those who "strive to ascend," does not mean as opponents but as going out to meet him, as the apostle says: to meet Christ.

At this too my heart was stunned: with wonder. And it was torn from its place: from the earthly things it used to delight in, so that it might be held upward toward the Lord. Hear the sound of terror and of his voice: from this point it is evident that he says these things in the Spirit. For he begins to say why his heart was torn from its place, namely by the authority of the gospel sounding terribly through the whole world: "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near." And at the roar of his mouth they go out: to those, that is, who are outside, among the delights of visible things. It goes round beneath the whole heaven, and its light is at the ends of the earth: as the church spreads through all nations. After it a voice will roar: after his first coming, the last trumpet of his second coming will thunder in glory. In the sound of his pride: he used "pride" for loftiness, because the first coming was in humility. And he cannot be searched out when his voice has been heard: so let the Lord be sought now, while he can be found, that is, grasped for salvation through unfeigned faith. Then it will not be possible, when he has come to judge and his voice has been heard saying, "Depart into the eternal fire," because the repentance of unbelievers will then be too late and fruitless. The mighty one will thunder wonderfully with his voice: because the voice of his first coming was not the voice of his strength but of our weakness, through his sharing in mortality. Of this it is said: "The weakness of God is stronger than men." For he did great things which we did not know: these things in the first coming; and therefore he will come afterward as judge to demand account of what he gave. "Which we did not know" is said in the person of those from whom the Lord's divinity was hidden, because they looked at the weakness of his flesh. Commanding the cloud: Be upon the earth: commanding his flesh, so that it might be received through the sacrament in remembrance of him, for the imitation of humility and the forming of love. And the storm of rain and the storm of showers of his power: the cloud is indeed upon the earth; but when it is pressed out to water hearts with the rain and showers of the word, which happens when the sacraments are understood, that lies not in our power but in his. He sets a sign in the hand of every man: through his works he shows him how guilty he is, so that every man may know his weakness and cry out: "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?" But the beasts went in under shelter and rested in their lair: sinners went in under the pardon of grace and rested in their conscience, their sins forgiven. From the storehouses comes a storm: temptation from the hidden order of things. And from the storehouses, cold: from secret places, judgment on those who do not persevere, so that their love grows cold because iniquity abounds. This rightly befalls them, since they place their hope not in God but in men. And from the Spirit of God ice will be given: not only will those who place their hope in men grow cold from [?] the abundance of the wicked; some also harden, as if with the ice of envy, at the good works of those in whom the Spirit of God is. To them Paul is the odor of death unto death. And who is sufficient for these things, to understand that it is right and just that ice is given by the Spirit of God? For just as carnal people who praise men grow cold through despair at men's wickedness, so carnal people who long to be praised by men harden through envy at men's righteousness. And he governs the water as it pleases him: so that he rains on one city and does not rain on another. This concerns the spiritual rain, given according to the merits of souls that submit or do not submit. And the cloud watered the grain: let us be grain, then, if we wish to be watered. He spread abroad the cloud, his light: the gospel of his incarnation. And it turns round about: it is handled throughout the whole world. With rudders, to do all that he has commanded them: the rudders by which that cloud is turned round about are the preachers of the word, through whom the churches are steered to do all the commandments of God. These things were established by him upon the earth: by our Lord Jesus Christ. Whether in the tribe or in his own land: whether in the tribe of Judah, from which he was born according to the flesh, and suffered, and rose again, and ascended into heaven (for from this tribe the apostles were born, and many brethren who were found near and were saved), whether called by him before his passion, or after his ascension through the apostles in Jerusalem itself and in the churches of Judea that were in Christ, as the apostle Paul recalls: "for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers." Or whether in mercy he willed it to be found: that is, he willed that cloud to be found in mercy by the Gentiles who believe. For this follows: "but that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy." Hear these things, Job: as though he renews attention, about to speak of the calling of the Gentiles. Stand, and be moved by the power of the Lord: do not be moved in mind by attributing anything to yourself. We know that God has established his works: rejecting, of course, those who glory in their own works. When he made light out of darkness: when he justified the ungodly; for "you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord." He knows the difference between the clouds: between evangelists, some of whom believed in him before the passion and others after the passion. And the enormous falls of the wicked: not of those who fell away by crucifying him, so that afterward they repented and were baptized in him, but the falls of those who could not be corrected and went on persecuting the church even afterward. Their falls are not small but enormous. But your robe is strong: proud dignity. This is said as if against one who dares to exalt himself on account of his own works. While the land from the south is at rest, will you with him make firm the heavens, which have been spread out for all alike to see? By the land from the south we fittingly understand those of the Jews who believed in Christ. For just as the sun is farther from a northern land and nearer to a southern one, so those whom the apostle calls "near" to the light of the evangelists are not unreasonably taken as the land from the south. And just as we usually take the heavens to mean the evangelists, as in "The heavens declare the glory of God" (for of them it is said, "Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world"), so we rightly take the lands to mean the peoples to whom the gospel has been preached. Now the peoples who believed from Judea came to rest when they departed from this earth; for they are not here now. Yet the authority of the evangelists has been made firm in the churches that come from the Gentiles, and made firm by the mercy of God, no longer aided by the authority of the churches of Judea which are in Christ. Therefore the sense here is to be pronounced as a question: Will you, while the land from the south is at rest, that is, when there is no longer in this life any Christian people from among the Jews, make firm with him the evangelists and the books of the divine Scriptures, which by God's mercy have been spread out for all alike to see, not for the Jews alone but for the Gentiles as well? He is commending the grace and mercy of God, so that no one may glory in merits, which was the pride of the Jews. Therefore teach me what we shall say to him, and let us rest from saying much: because, once convicted, they have nothing to say to him except that they have no merit of their own but need his mercy. Do you stand by me as a book or a scribe, so that I may stand and make a man keep silent? Why then do you not speak, if you have something to say? For you are not taking down my words as though I were dictating, so that you yourself say nothing; we are surely conversing. But the light that shines back from the clouds is not visible to all: he returns to what he was saying about the hope of forgiveness of sins and the illumination of grace through the mercy of God. For the light shines back from the clouds, yet it does not belong to the clouds themselves: they are illuminated. It is one thing to shine with one's own light, another to shine back because one has been lit up. But this is not visible to all; for many think that souls shine with their own light when they are wise. From these come those who, "claiming to be wise, became fools." And the wind passes and will cleanse them: here he means the wind of which it is said, "At the rebuke of the blast of your anger," and, "Where shall I flee from your Spirit?" For through the chastenings of temptations men are shown what they deserve: that by their sins they are themselves darkness and lack the glory of God. So they come to wish to be lit by his light, giving honor to him, not to themselves, and thus, having laid aside their pride, are cleansed from great transgression. For the Spirit of sanctification does not pass, but remains. From the north come clouds the color of gold: they come from the most wicked ungodliness, far removed from God, and yet they are converted, cleansed, and illuminated with wisdom. How? Only through grace, by which merits are not considered but sins are forgiven. Hence the one who wished to be pardoned said: "I will teach the wicked your ways, and the ungodly will turn to you," like clouds from the east or the north, now golden in color because their darkness has been lit up. In these is the great glory and honor of the Almighty: the one who is forgiven most loves most, since he who is almighty can justify even the ungodly. And we have found no other like him in power: for he alone committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. For God alone is truthful, but every man is a liar; and so God made man prevailed when he was judged. Do you not think that he who judges justly will hear? So let no one, despairing of pardon, add sins to sins, as though already consigned to damnation because he is sure of God's justice, under which he cannot go unpunished. For God judges justly in such a way that he also hears those who beg for pardon, and all the more so the more justly he judges. For it is not just judgment to lump together the penitent who make supplication with those who refuse humility and the satisfaction of penance. Therefore men will fear him: if they remember that they are men by confessing their sins, since they are still men. To them it is said: "Are you not men?" The wise in heart will also fear him: lest by attributing to themselves what they have received, and by claiming to be wise, they become fools. For what is given to the humble can be taken away from the proud. Therefore, even the wise, though they are wise through the illumination of the heart and not through boasting of the tongue, and are kings who judge the earth spiritually while they themselves are judged by no one, should still serve the Lord in fear and rejoice with trembling, lest they perish from the right way. For it is God who works in them both to will and to work for his good pleasure.

And after Elihu had stopped speaking, the Lord spoke to Job through the whirlwind of the cloud. Even if this voice came in the same way as it came to Moses, or as when the Lord showed himself to three disciples on the mountain, still it does not say simply "through the cloud" but "through the whirlwind of the cloud." I think this means that Job was questioned, that is, tested, not through sound flesh but through the affliction and turmoil of the flesh. Who is this who hides counsel from me, keeping words in his heart, and thinks he is hidden from me? So no one should say that he suffers something harsh undeservedly. If one does not sin in deeds, one at least sins in words; and if not in words, then at least by rash presumption within, in the heart or in the words of one's thoughts. Since these things are not hidden from God, let no one who is scourged say that he is disciplined unjustly, as though there were nothing further in which he could advance through that discipline. For we must understand that Job was praised by God's testimony to the devil at the beginning of this book, and to his three friends at the end, in such a way that God still knew how much he lacked for perfection. A father's scourges lead toward that perfection even men who are praiseworthy by the standard of this life and already pleasing to God.
