God would not remove these scourges from the apostle, but said: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness. Gird up your loins like a man: this signifies that God's servants suffer hard and bitter things in this world so that they may gather in and bind up all their affections, which would otherwise flow away into earthly pleasures. I will question you, and you answer me: Where were you when I founded the earth? From here he now begins to commend the preeminence of our Lord Jesus Christ. In him is the salvation of all who were struck by the serpent's poisoned persuasion, so that no one should think his salvation lies in himself. For he is God, not in the sense in which it was said, You are gods and sons of the Most High, but as one for whom it is not robbery to be equal to the Father. He is Son of Man, not like the sons of men in whom there is no salvation, but above his companions. For he is not only righteous, as Job, Paul and the Church are, but also the one who makes righteous, as the only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth. Two things must be brought out. One is what sets his divine humanity apart: in him the prince of this world found nothing, for in his passion he was then paying back what he had not stolen. The other is the justification of the saints through the forgiveness of sins. These saints, gathered into one, become his body, the Church. Job is a small part of that Church according to the history, because he was justified, and he is also a figure of the whole Church. So he begins to say prophetically what he is about to say. Where were you when I founded the earth? Is this because he did not yet exist, or because the earth was not founded through him, as it was through the only Son? And is this earth meant, or the Church herself? For it is the Church that received the cornerstone, which he will speak of shortly. Tell me, if you have knowledge: for the things the Lord did for us in time belong to knowledge. Who set its measures, if you know? This is according to the distribution of spiritual gifts. For grace has been given to each of us according to the measure of Christ's gift. That is why it says: Ascending on high he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to men. For if the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? It is according to the measure of each part that the body grows and builds itself up in love. Or who stretched a line over it? He did so in order to make it his inheritance, distinguishing it from those to whom he says: I do not know you. For the Lord knows those who are his. Or on what are its rings fixed? The divine books bind it together so that it does not fall apart, and they are fixed upon the Lord. Anyone who tries to interpret them without him must drift and go astray. And who is it that laid the cornerstone upon it? The one whom the builders rejected. When the stars were made together: so many thousands baptized together by the word of life, shining among sinners as though in darkness. All my angels praised me with a loud voice: the evangelists. I shut in the sea with gates: the peoples made bitter by love of earthly things. But why with gates? Perhaps so that the sea would not only have a limit on how far it could test the righteous with persecutions, but also so that the righteous might be able to go out from it. When it raged, wanting to burst forth from its mother's womb: when it grew angry in the council of the city of Babylon, which commits fornication through love of this world. It wanted to extend its persecutions so as to destroy from the earth those of whom it was said: I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you take them away from evil. I set a cloud around it as a covering: for not only the good but also many who are bad and love this world have submitted to the sacrament of Christ's body, and its authority restrains them from persecuting the saints. And I wrapped it in mist: that is, in the ignorance by which they expect earthly happiness from it and fear earthly misfortune. For this reason they fear those whom they would otherwise persecute. For it was not only said: The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and those who seek the Lord shall praise him. It was also said: All the rich of the earth have eaten and worshipped. And I set bounds for it, putting bars and gates. The bounds hold its savagery in check, not so that it afflicts no one, but so that its testing goes only so far. The bars keep the unrighteous from advancing, and the gates let the righteous go out from among them. And I said: Thus far you shall come, and you shall not pass beyond. Just as the devil himself was given a limit on how far he could afflict Job, so that sea was given a limit on how far it could persecute the Church. But your waves shall be broken within yourself: by the mutual devastation of discords and wars. Or did I establish the morning light with you? That is: did I predestine the time of the resurrection by your counsel? Or did the morning star know its order? Here we must supply "with you?" He calls the Lord the morning star because his rising at the resurrection came at dawn. For it could not have been said of anyone else: and may the morning star rise in your hearts. He knew his order: to be the firstfruits of those who sleep, the firstborn from the dead, the head of the Church, with his body to follow in the future resurrection of the saints. To grasp the wings of the earth? It was said: If I take up my wings straight on. These wings are the spiritual powers of the faithful, which lift them above worldly enticements. To shake the wicked out of it? He knew his order and rose first, so long beforehand, for this purpose: to instill faith in the resurrection. Through those very wings of the Church, by the ministry of messengers flying everywhere, he has been preached in every place, so that he may rightly take hold of them for the work of judging the twelve tribes of Israel. He will do this when he comes to shake the wicked out of the Church, for now, before the judgment, they are tolerated in its midst. And did you take clay from the earth and fashion a living creature? He may be recalling Adam himself. Or he may mean that now, in the sixth age of the world, just as then on the sixth day, man has been made out of sinners, as out of the clay of the earth, according to the image of the one who created him. The Church certainly did not do this. Rather, in this she herself was made, through the Word made flesh at the fitting time, through whom all things were made. And did you set him on the earth in renown? This man, made in the sixth age of the world, was set on the earth with more renown than the one made on the sixth day. Before that one, there were as yet no other people through whom his fame could spread, unless perhaps he is called renowned because he has now become known in this way. And did you take away light from the wicked? As he did who came so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind. Or did you break the arm of the proud? That is, their power, as he did who chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong. Or did you come to the source of the sea? As he did: when he came, whatever was hidden in the hearts of the wicked was laid open to him through their confession, and they were justified by believing in him. For what can the source of the sea better mean than that hidden place from which all this most bitter wickedness bursts forth? It stirs up huge waves of evil deeds that are now open to view. People see these in open acts, but they cannot see the source itself. Or do you walk in the tracks of the abyss? Here the abyss is rightly understood as worldly life, all that lies in the depth of evils. As it is written, the sinner, when he comes there, shows contempt. But even the most hopeless have submitted to grace, been saved through the forgiveness of sins, and come up out of it. They have received Christ, not into the abyss that weighed them down, but in its place. So where the abyss used to walk, trampling them, Christ dwelling in them now walks in the tracks of the abyss. These tracks remain in the memory of their sins, so that as they recall where they had been, they may love the more the one they have received, by whom so much has been forgiven them. Or are the gates of death opened to you in fear? The gates of death are opened to all who die, but not in fear. They opened in fear only to the one who died in order to destroy death. Or, at any rate, they are opened for rising again. Or did the gatekeepers of hell fear when they saw you? As they feared that one alone, in whom the prince of the world found nothing deserving death. They let him go so quickly, and they had admitted him unwillingly. The gatekeepers of hell should be understood as certain lower powers set over death. Have you understood the breadth beneath heaven? As he understood it who spread the Church throughout it. Tell me, then, how great each thing is: for who could know this except someone he has taught? Or in what land does light dwell? He teaches this, for the disclosure of his words gives light and gives understanding to little ones. Or what is the place of darkness? He teaches this too, who says: Come to him and be enlightened. In this he shows that those who withdraw grow dark, since they do not want to be little ones. For the beginning of human pride is to fall away from God. So those who did not glorify God or give thanks became futile in their thoughts, their senseless heart was darkened, and they became the place of darkness. Or perhaps the place of darkness is the one that receives those who persist in their sins, so that they themselves are the darkness, and that place, which truly no one knows, is its place. Similarly, the land where light dwells can be understood as that land of the living, that is, the blessedness that will receive those who persevere in faith, hope and love, who were once darkness but now are light in the Lord. If you could lead me to their boundaries? That is, how far those who are such reach. For where is the wisdom of God not present, which reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly? Certainly no human being can be compared to it. And if you also know their paths, do you know that you were born then, and that the number of your years is great? Suppose you do know the paths of the wicked, who are either darkness or the place of darkness. Indeed, all, even those now converted to God, walked in those very paths before they received from God the grace that justifies the ungodly. Even so, do you know that the cause of your mortal birth into this world arose at the moment when the first parents of humankind set out on those same paths? Made wicked by their transgression, they summoned death with hands and words, so that all die in Adam. For the number of a person's years should not be reckoned, so small, from when he appeared in this life, but from when the first mortal birth took place. For example, when Abraham was born, all the Hebrews were born in him. So for each person the number of years is great, measured from the origin of mortality, which arose in the paths of the wicked. But who remembers that he existed, or could know when he existed that he was in his father's loins? No one even recalls the time when he was born, not in his parents, but in himself, and yet no one doubts that at that time he already existed, lived and felt. But that wisdom which forms all things knows all things, not only those above the heavens but also these mortal things. And since Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, he knows these things. He too was born mortal, not by mortal necessity, for he was free among the dead, but out of compassion for mortals, to set them free from death. Or have you entered the storehouses of the snow? That is: have you attained to such knowledge as he had, who knew even the fitting causes of impending stumbling blocks, though they are secret and hidden? For this is why they are called storehouses: they are kept for testing and exercising the hearts of the spiritual. He cried out about this: Woe to the world because of stumbling blocks! For stumbling blocks must come; but woe to that man through whom the stumbling block comes! Those lifted up high by pride freeze like snow and fall, and because their wickedness abounds, the love of many grows cold. But those who wait for the Lord, acting courageously and fervent in spirit, will persevere to the end and be saved. Or have you seen the storehouses of the hail? Those wicked people are hail when they are not only sluggish, with no fervor of spirit, but also batter others with stubborn hardness, persecuting and assailing them. Which are stored up for you for the time of enemies and for the day of fighting and war? From this alone, who would not see whose person Job bears in prophecy? These things are not stored up for this one man for the time of enemies and the day of fighting and war, but surely for God's one people. The time of enemies lasts until wickedness passes away. The more wickedness abounds, the more fiercely we must fight and wage war against the devil, so that the love of those who persevere does not grow cold. And where does the frost come from? Who knows this? Perhaps only that these things are like the beginnings of birth pangs, for frost is the tiniest hail. And is the south wind scattered beneath heaven? Although mortal flesh feels the south wind as oppressive, I do not recall it ever signifying anything evil in the holy books, just as the north wind never signifies anything good. The south wind blows from the quarter where the light shines, the north wind from the quarter farthest from the light. So the south wind is scattered beneath heaven to signify some help from God against all those kinds of wickedness, as long as we are not yet in heaven but beneath heaven. Who prepared the river of the heavy rain, and a path for the voices of the storm? See how briefly three things are summed up here. The Lord lists them among the temptations: those who build on the rock can scorn them, but they are ruinous to those who build on the sand. He mentioned the rain, the river and the voices of the storm, by which we understand the winds. A person is tempted by the rain when he misunderstands the very loftiness of the divine Scriptures and takes it as an occasion for sinning. Hearing, for instance, To whom little is forgiven, loves little, he says to himself, Let us do evil so that good may come, and he remains in sin so that grace may abound. There are many such passages by which people overthrow themselves, misinterpreting God's word and promising themselves impunity when the divine books commend mercy. A person is tempted by the river when the temptation comes from people who have understood and received these things in that way. By the river he now means what collects from the rain and is called a torrent, when he says: Who prepared the river of the heavy rain? That is, who prepared what it would fill and where it would run? These are the vessels of wrath made ready for destruction, which take the Scriptures in the way I have described. Through them that ruinous interpretation, which fruitful fields do not take in, runs more freely. The more it seems to come from divine authority, the greater the force with which it drives, throws down and sweeps away whatever it finds unstable. A person is tempted by the winds when he is puffed up by the empty persuasions of proud men, that is, men who throw about empty words on their own authority. So whoever is being prepared for destruction by God's judgment, because he does not obey his words, which is building on sand, cannot withstand such winds. By falling, he becomes a path for the voices of the storm. I think "heavy rain" was said in the sense of "hard to grasp," that is, hard to understand. To rain on a land where there is no man. Here we must supply "Who prepared?" By "man" he seems to mean the law that was given to the Jews. So we understand this as the shower of the gospel upon the Gentiles. In the desert where there is no human being: among the Gentiles themselves, where there was no authority of anyone who knew God. To satisfy the trackless and uninhabitable land and make the green grass spring up: many are the children of the desolate woman, more than of her who has a husband. In all four of these verses we must supply: Who prepared? Who is the father of the rain? Such as the Bridegroom, who sent his sons to water the earth with the preaching of the kingdom of heaven. And who gave birth to the clods of dew? Those who receive that preaching well. He says "clods of dew" in the way one speaks of wine vessels, made for the purpose of holding wine. From whose womb does the ice come forth? Is ice to be taken in a good sense, because of its firmness and its being held back from flowing? Then "From whose womb does the ice come forth?" would be said in the same way as "Who is the father of the rain?" Or is "womb" used for a hidden place, so that the ice comes forth from his womb in the sense that God gave them over to a depraved mind? Or rather, does the ice come forth from the womb of the one who, by urging the wickedness with which he is filled within, makes people grow cold and hard once they have lost the warmth of love? For who knew him as he did who said to those hard and resistant to the gospel: You are of your father the devil? Or who gave birth to the frost in the sky? It comes down like a river of water. I think that what we took to be the last meaning for the ice should be applied to the frost too. Yet "in the sky" was not added for nothing. It means that the frost comes from those who are in charge, who imitate good messengers of truth and disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness. This is the point of the further phrase: it comes down like a river of water. Or who made the face of the wicked waste away? That is, put it to shame. Who? Only he who also glorified those whom he justified. Or have you understood the bonds of the Pleiades, and opened the enclosure of Orion? Will you open Mazzaroth in its season, and bring the Evening Star over its building? Must we also investigate astrology to learn the properties of these stars before we can understand this passage? I would be surprised if that suited our discourse, and it would certainly take far too long, so let us move on to other matters. Or, since certain stars are named here, are all the stars to be understood by the figure of speech in which the whole is understood from a part? That holds provided Mazzaroth is a star; we have not found it translated even in the Greek, for it is clear enough that the name is Hebrew. The whole is also understood from a part in what is written: Before the morning star I begot you. The morning star was not created first in all creation, so that "before the morning star" would mean "before all creation." Rather, the morning star stands for all the stars, which is a part for the whole, and all the stars stand for all times, for it is written of the stars: and let them be for signs and for seasons. In this way the Lord is shown to have been born before all times, certainly not born in time, and therefore coeternal with the Father. So the mention of the Pleiades, Orion, Mazzaroth and the Evening Star leads us to understand, in shorthand, all the stars together. If this is allowed with the morning star alone, how much more may the rest be understood through this kind of expression when so many are named! Why, then, does it say in one place "have you understood the bonds," in another "have you opened," in another "will you open in its season," and in another "will you bring over its building"? Are these phrases proper to each of the stars named in turn? Or could one just as rightly say "you opened the enclosure of the Pleiades" and "you understood the bonds of Orion"? The other two could be interchanged in the same way, as in the psalm: He who dwells in heaven will laugh at them, and the Lord will mock them. The sense would lose nothing if it were said: He who dwells in heaven will mock them, and the Lord will laugh at them. For just as he who dwells in heaven is the Lord himself, so the name of the Pleiades and the name of Orion mean the same thing, if either one stands for all the stars. So by the name of all the stars we should understand all those in the Church whose way of life is in heaven. Their bonds are the ties by which they are joined to one another and to God, so that they do not fall. And love never falls. Who would have known this unless he had shown it, who says: I give you a new commandment, that you love one another, and: Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father? Their enclosure is the divine Scripture, which fences them in and which they do not overstep. And who opens it, except the one to whom we turn so that the veil may be taken away? The season for opening them, that is, for displaying and revealing them, is when the Lord comes and will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and reveal the thoughts of the heart; and then each one will receive praise from God. He alone will do this in his season, for when he, our life, appears, then we too will appear with him in glory. And he will bring them over their building, for he will make them possess what they have built here. For if the work anyone has built upon it survives, he will receive a reward. Do you know the changes of the sky? Changes for the worse, like those who knew God but did not glorify him as God? They refused to be the seat of God, and so they were changed when they became futile in their thoughts. Or changes for the better? For we shall all rise again, but we shall not all be changed. Who will be changed is clear when he says: and we shall be changed. For when the righteous are changed, the sky will be changed, since heaven is God's throne. The Word of God is wisdom, and the Word was God, and the soul of the righteous is the throne of wisdom. Or rather both kinds? For he did not say "the change" of the sky but "the changes." Or all the things that happen together beneath the sky? Just as changes in the sky affect what is beneath the sky, so too when the righteous are changed, whether for the worse or for the better, they affect carnal people in either direction. Will you call the cloud with your voice? Either with the inner voice, or with the voice that said: Follow me, or with the voice that said: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? And will mighty waters obey you with trembling? Mighty peoples do so when they hear: Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you both to will and to act for his good pleasure. Will you send rivers with force, and will they go? Rivers of living water, he says, will flow from his belly. By "force" he means the confidence that kept them from fearing their persecutors, for those who use force seize the kingdom of heaven. Or will they say to you: What is it? That is, will they ask you either what you want them to do, as Saul said: What do you command me to do? or what reward they may hope for, as they said: See, we have left everything and followed you; what then will there be for us? Who gave women skill in weaving and knowledge of varied colors? In Solomon, too, the woman weaves garments for her husband. So this should be understood as the works of the churches, by which God is honored. For the weaving itself is the greatest and most distinctive work of the churches: to bind together the weak brothers, like a soft, fluffy weft, by interweaving them with the firm and upright spiritual ones, who are like the warp threads. And the knowledge of varied colors serves this purpose: just as in a many-colored fabric the variety of colors does not spoil the beauty of its unity, so among the brothers the gifts should differ in such a way that they hold together without any discord of envy, bearing with one another in love and striving to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Or who numbers the clouds in wisdom? For the Lord knows those who are his. But which human being, he says, knows this? And did he bend the instruments of heaven down to earth? These are the heavenly angels, through whom divine utterances are usually announced. They did not fall like that one angel, but bent down to earth in obedience, above all when the Lord himself was on earth. For the evangelist says: and the angels ministered to him. But ash has been spread out like earth, and he has fastened him like food to stones. The humility of repentance has been spread widely and abundantly. Its purpose is that the Lord, who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble, might cling to them as if with the glue of love, a man to men, in order to be the mediator between God and men. He gives himself to them as food through the sacrament of his body and blood, choosing the foolish things of the world, like stones, to shame the wise. For he is food to the angels insofar as he is the Word of God with God; but so that he might be food for stones, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. So he will be fastened to human beings when repentance goes first, as if ash were spread out to make a way for him. Hence the one who said: Bear fruit worthy of repentance, and do not say to yourselves, We have Abraham as our father, for God is able to raise up children to Abraham from these stones. He was proclaiming the stones to which the Lord would be fastened as food. But if the humility of repentance does not go first, he will not be fastened, because he knows the lofty from afar. Will you catch prey for the lion, or fill the appetites of the dragons? It was said of the devil: and you will trample the lion and the dragon, because of his ambushes and his rage. So all his angels are compared to lions and dragons. The one who catches prey for them and fills their appetites is the one who convicts people of their wickedness and hands them over to the devil's power. For they want their wickedness to stay hidden. But when it is brought out, they are certainly caught, so that they fall into the power of the devil and his angels, with whom they agreed. For they cower in their dens: in the hiding places of their ambushes. If they did not cower, who could stand? They tremble at his command, under which they cried out: Why have you come before the time to destroy us? And just as it is clear that they would not have entered the pigs unless they had been permitted, so we must understand that they can do nothing against anyone unless they are permitted. They are permitted by the justice that governs all things, whether for the sake of testing or of punishment, which is inflicted either to condemn or to correct. And they sit in the woods lying in wait: for the will to do harm never rests in them, even when they are not given the power. In their ambushes, amid so dense a forest of carnal opportunities, they watch for anyone who is caught by the divine laws, that is, convicted of his sin, so that he deserves to be counted as their prey. But who prepared food for the raven? For its young cry to the Lord, wandering and seeking food, as in the psalm: and to the young ravens that call upon him. This passage is very like that verse. They cannot be understood in a bad sense, since they call upon him. So they stand for those who are black, that is, sinners not yet washed white by the forgiveness of sins. But they are young because they are already humble, and wandering because they have not yet come to know the truth, though they seek it devoutly when they cry to the Lord. Food can be prepared for the raven because of the foreknowledge of him who knows that each person, even one not yet humble, will be converted. Yet it is the young, that is, the humble, who cry to the Lord.

Do you know the time for bringing forth rocks for the goat-stags? In Greek, *tragos* means a he-goat and *elaphos* a deer, so the goat-stag is an animal made up of a goat and a deer. It signifies, then, a mind that serves the law of God according to the inner man, but which, insofar as it is still partly a goat, sees another law in its members, warring against the law of its mind and taking it captive to the law of sin. For such as these, at the proper time, rocks were brought forth by him who set firm foundations of examples in the Scriptures. Resting on these, those whose flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh need not despair of themselves. In time, once the deer's vigor has overcome the serpent's enticements, they will live by the Spirit and follow the Spirit, so that sin, from which the likeness to the goat is drawn, may not reign in their mortal body to make them obey its desires. Or have you watched over the births of the hinds? This means the churches, in the persons of the spiritual, who with a mother's affection persuade others to imitate them, and whom serpentine opinions can no longer harm. Yet even such as these are watched over, for they rely not on themselves but on God. And have you numbered the months of their bearing? For they give birth only through the gospel, which the Lord preached with the authority of his teaching for a fixed number of months, from his baptism to his passion and ascension. And have you eased their pains? For it was not said without pain: My children, with whom I am in labor again until Christ is formed in you. These pains are eased when the birth has taken place, that is, when the truth has won over those for whom there is such groaning, the word of God bringing this about in the depths of the conscience. And have you reared their fawns without fear? They are not timid, nourished on the milk of the sacraments; for they have not received the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear. You will send out their offspring: into the freedom of richer spiritual pasture. Their young will break off the chains of worldly desires. They will multiply on wheat: on the more solid food of wisdom after the nourishment of milk. They will go out and not return to them: they will go out, as it were, from the narrow confines of the teaching that is handed on to beginners through human teachers; and they will not return to their mothers, since they no longer need milk or require human teachers. These three verses, of course, are not to be read as questions. Who is it that has let the wild ass go free? It would be surprising if by the wild ass he did not mean those few who serve God free from all business. And who has loosed his bonds? The bonds of carnal and worldly affections. For I have made the desert his dwelling and the salt land his tents. From there he may cry: My soul has thirsted for you. Mocking the crowd of the city: the city that Scripture calls Babylon, walking along the broad road that leads to destruction. And not hearing the complaint of the tax collector: for he owes nothing to anyone. He has surveyed the mountains of his pasture: the greatness of the revelations. And he searches after every green thing: after everything that is everlasting. Will the unicorn be willing to serve you? This is one who is proud in the dignity of this world. For Christ has subdued even such men and made them ministers of the church; *monoceros* means 'one-horned', which signifies pride. Or to sleep at your manger? At the lowliness of him who was even laid as an infant in a manger, one rests in the security of the forgiveness of sins and forgets the cares of a bad conscience. And will he bind his yoke with thongs? He bears the light yoke bound with thongs, that is, by the authority of those who have put the flesh to death and tamed it. That is why John too was girded with a leather belt, and not with the rough ropes of sins. Or will he plow furrows for you in the plain? He will open the hearts of an obedient people to win the kingdom of God. Do you trust him because his strength has been changed? So that he no longer seeks the vanity of human praise and honor, even in the ministry of the church, as he sought it in the world. Or will you entrust your works to him? This is like the one in whose stead the apostle says he serves as ambassador, urging people on Christ's behalf to be reconciled to God. And will you believe him that he will give you back your sowing? He will claim none of it for his own dominion; by 'sowing' he means the work of sowing. And will he bring it into your threshing floor? So that he may be among those whom the Lord himself tells to ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest, and may not want to make a threshing floor for himself. That is what the founder of heresies and schisms does, and everyone who seeks not God's glory but his own. For it is very hard to make this unicorn willing. Yet even this is granted and brought about in a man's soul by him who alone does wonders, destroying counsels and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and taking every understanding captive to obey him. The feather of the ostriches is mingled with the wings of the heron and the hawk. By this verse we should understand that the slow-witted are given a gift through the grace of him who chose the foolish things of the world. The ostriches signify them, since they cannot fly. The gift is that they are made equal to the swiftness of the clever who believe alongside them, and these clever believers are signified by the birds he mentioned. And she has left her eggs on the ground: here he begins to speak of the ostrich, that is, of those whom he signifies by this animal. Their slow feathers would not be mingled with the wings of swift birds so that they fly together, unless they left on the ground their former hope, which he signifies by the eggs. And they are warmed in the dust: for even though he no longer pays attention to what he used to hope for in the world, it often comes to him anyway through the favor of the lovers of the world, who are compared to dust. And she has forgotten that a foot will scatter them and a beast of the field will trample them: someone's hostile greed and the unjust of this world may disturb and crush such a hope of his, like the eggs she leaves on the ground. If so, he cares so little that he does not feel it, as if he had forgotten. She has hardened herself against her young, as if they were not hers: even when it is no longer a hope, like the eggs, but the thing itself, like young already hatched, that is, temporal happiness, he resolutely despises it. He does not want it as his happiness, because he longs for the true one. She labored in vain, without any fear: this refers to the time before he is converted. For then he labors without fruit in worldly hope, and, more foolishly still, without any fear, since he presumes upon uncertain things. Because God has disregarded her in wisdom and has not given her a share of understanding: for what is more foolish than to trust in vanity and toil to acquire perishable things without any fear of losing them? Many people take on this attitude when long worldly prosperity has come their way, especially if it has come down in unbroken succession from grandfathers and great-grandfathers, so that they do not believe they could suddenly become unhappy. And because they usually appear great on earth, yet do not enjoy a heavenly way of life on the wings of virtue, they are rightly compared to ostriches. But note what follows: When the time comes, she will fly up on high and laugh at the horse and its rider. After the fullness of time came, the rich of this world were commanded not to be haughty and not to hope in uncertain riches, but in the living God. Then they began to lift up their hearts to the Lord and to laugh at the proud persecutors, whom the Lord has cast into the sea. For then the ostrich's feather, mingled with the swift birds, makes for the sky, and the other things said above about this animal come to pass. Did you clothe the horse with strength? He seems to describe a martyr, a fearless and eager witness to the saving faith, strong not by his own strength but by the strength with which the Lord has clothed him. And did you set neighing in his neck? Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand firm on the evil day. And boldness as the glory of his breast? This is the boldness with which Isaiah dares to speak. The glory of the breast is a conscience that proves a man's work, so that each may have his glory in himself and not in another. Going out into the plain he frolics: coming out into the light of freedom, he exults in the breadth of love and does good works with ease. And he goes forth to battle with strength: against the trials of adversity. And meeting the javelin he scorns it: because armor has been put around him, and part of it is the shield of faith, on which the flaming darts of the enemy are quenched. Nor does he turn away from the sword: either from visible death, or from those who are both hard in refusing to assent to the truth and sharp in persecuting. He does not turn away from them, since he is commanded to love even them. For over him bow and sword rejoice: for his confession asserts two things. One is God's threat, which foretells invisible punishments from afar. The other is the testimony of the word, by which he overcomes all errors as if at close quarters. It is one thing to threaten that the punishments of sinners lie far in the future, which is like aiming arrows with a bow; it is another to fight hand to hand and overcome present desires with the sword of the word. With the trembling of lance and spear: what does it mean that bow and sword rejoice over him with the trembling of lance and spear? Perhaps it means this. Unless he too trembles, that is, fears the future death that divine justice hurls, he cannot despise the present death that the persecutor threatens. Only so will his confession be fearless and will he preach with confidence the truth that enemies cannot resist. And so 'they rejoice over him', that is, through him God's teaching is freely asserted, and by that teaching God threatens the ungodly with future destruction and slays present wickedness. For unless the joy of our hope were joined to a trembling at damnation, our very security would be careless and proud presumption, and the psalm would not say to us: Rejoice in him with trembling. And in his anger he overturns the earth: he is angry with himself so as to overturn within himself the earthly desires and carnal fears that turn a person away from enduring suffering. Perhaps this is the sense in which it was said: Be angry and do not sin. For each one ought to rebuke and correct himself with a most wholesome anger, saying: Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you disturb me? Hope in God, for I will confess him. And because confession is made with the mouth for salvation, there follows at once: the salvation of my face, my God. And he will not believe until the trumpet sounds: for before the time of temptation, even if earthly fear has been overturned, it does not show, nor should it be readily believed, until the time of temptation itself has proved it. But when the trumpet sounds, he will say, 'Aha!': when the time of temptation comes, then indeed his soul will please him, if he glories in tribulations. For tribulation produces patience, patience proof, and proof hope. Then he no longer says angrily to his soul, Why do you disturb me? Instead he says in glorying: Praise the Lord, my soul. And he smells the battle from afar: not as though it were in the persecuting men who can be seen, but from afar, that is, far from the eyes. He knows that his struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities and powers and the rulers of the world of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places; this is the meaning of 'from afar'. 'Smells' is aptly said because of the prince of the power of this air, for odors, good or bad, are perceived by smell. So the one who smells the battle is the one who understands that the prince of the power of this air is at work in the children of unbelief. He suffers their wrath and snares as they persecute him, and so he fights against the spiritual forces of wickedness with spiritual weapons. He does not fight with bodily weapons against flesh and blood, that is, against the wicked and lost men whom he sees with the eyes of the flesh. The thunder of the captains and the shouting: 'he smells' is to be understood. I think 'thunder' is said because of the air itself, in which these same spiritual forces of wickedness move. These spirits are not called rulers of the world because they rule heaven and earth, but in the sense that the apostle himself explains. Lest it be understood in that way, he immediately added what he meant by rulers of the world: 'of this darkness', he says, that is, of the ungodly. To them, once they have turned to the Lord, he says: For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. For it lies in each person's will whether he is darkness or light. When he is darkness, he is so in himself, that is, in the sins that are his own. When he is light, he is so not in himself but in the Lord, by whom he is enlightened, so that, as Isaiah says, his darkness may be like noonday. It is also said in the Psalms: You will light up my darkness. So those whom the apostle calls rulers of darkness are called captains in this verse. For the darkness, that is, the ungodly, is led by them to persecute the godly. The godly are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake, not those who suffer for their own impieties and iniquities. And he says that the martyr smells the shouting of such captains. This is not because any sound from there is heard with the ears of the body, but because, through faith, they cry out to the ears of the heart how much the devil and his angels are plotting against God's servants. Hence the apostle says: For we are not ignorant of his designs. To this shouting of the captains the ears of unbelievers are surely deaf. Is it by your wisdom that the hawk grows its feathers? Just so, in the wisdom of God, which is Christ, the new man is gradually renewed, so that his way of life will be in heaven. With wings spread, unmoving, looking toward the south? The virtues of the twofold love are unfolded, free from every worldly hindrance, and he remains unshaken in faith. Yet even in this he does not presume on himself. He hopes in God and turns his attention back to him from whom the very ardor of love is breathed in, so that he may keep his strength for him, saying: Shall not my soul be subject to God? For from him comes my salvation; for he is my God and my savior, my protector; I shall be moved no more. And is it at your command that the eagle mounts up? It mounts at the command of him who said: When I am lifted up, I will draw all things to myself. For he was about to die for us and to raise his body by resurrection into heaven, and he says: Wherever the carcass is, there the eagles will gather. For he has satisfied with heavenly good things the desire of the one whose youth will be renewed like the eagle's. The eagle's mounting up can also refer to what the apostle says: For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God. In that case the following verse, about the vulture, refers to what follows there as well: if we are of sound mind, it is for you. For there follows: Or will the vulture stay, sitting on its nest on the rock? This seems to describe a disposition not to contemplate sublime things in the mind's ecstasy, but to care for those below through the temperance by which one adapts to human affairs. The aim is that the ungodly, who are counted as dead, may be justified through the word, that is, devoured as it were by the mouth, and so be changed into the body of the church. For the vulture feeds on the dead. That is why it says 'on its nest', where it lays the works necessary for this life as if they were its young. And it says 'on the rock' because, after the apostle said, if we are of sound mind, it is for you, he immediately added: For the love of Christ compels us; and the rock was Christ. And 'it will stay sitting' fits well with what is said: I am hard pressed between the two, having the desire to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. This part refers to the eagle's mounting up. To the vulture sitting and staying in its nest belongs the rest: but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake. The whole church, too, is rightly understood as the rock, also because of Simon, who for this reason was named Peter by the Lord. So the summit of the rock is the head of the church. To this is added the verse that follows: On the summit of the rock, and in a hollow? 'Summit' refers to what is the head, while 'hollow' refers to the fact that our life is hidden with Christ in God. And when it is there, it seeks food: of which it was said to Peter, Kill and eat, so that he might incorporate into the church those of the Gentiles who would believe. Its eyes look far ahead, and its young wallow in blood: in the hope of future immortality he directs his aim far ahead, toward eternal life. Yet his works wallow in the weakness of the flesh, that is, they are tossed by doubtful movements, since human ignorance cannot be sure which of the things he does in mercy will profit whom toward God. Even so, with eyes looking far ahead to eternal salvation, he dispenses them with sincere love. Such a worker and dispenser may find people who have already died to this world through the disposition by which they renounce the devil. When he does, he offers them without any hesitation the ministry of his mouth in the work of preaching, by which he may carry them, now fully prepared, into the body of the church. And therefore there follows: Wherever there are carcasses, they are found at once.

The Lord answered Job and said. The fact that the Lord now resumes speaking, as it were, though he himself had been the one speaking, is taken to mean that Job was struck dumb at what had been said and fell silent, so that he dared say nothing more. So in the next two verses the Lord urges him to reply. Does the one who disputes with the Almighty keep quiet? That is: why do you keep quiet when you are disputing with the Almighty? Will one who reproves God answer like this? Here we must supply "surely not," so that the sense is: surely one who answers in a dispute is not reproving God? For a person disputes with the Almighty by asking questions, not by proving him wrong or refuting him. So the fact that he is almighty is no reason to stop disputing with him. Nor is anyone expected to reprove him by disputing, since he is Truth itself. It can also be understood this way: Does the one who disputes with the Lord find rest? That is: since the one who disputes with the Almighty does not find rest, one should not dispute with him if one wants to find rest. For a disputant usually contradicts, and whoever contradicts God cannot find rest; that is, he finds no rest unless he agrees with God's will without any contradiction. For one who reproves God will answer like this; that is, when someone answers God by disputing, he reproves God and therefore does not reach rest. Hence the saying: O man, who are you to answer back to God? But what had Job done of this kind? For God does not regard him as one contradicting him, as his friends did in their lack of understanding, since God bears such witness to him both at the beginning of the book and at the end. Or was this said because of the person Job represented, that is, the body of the Lord, which is the Church? In the Church there is a large share of the weak: not those who have despaired, but those still in danger as they make their way forward, whose feet are almost moved and whose steps have nearly slipped as they envy sinners, seeing the peace that sinners enjoy. These people say: How does God know? Is there knowledge in the Most High? Look, these are sinners, yet they prosper in the world and have gained riches. Was it for nothing that I kept my heart righteous and washed my hands among the innocent, and was scourged all day long, and my rebuke came every morning? Indeed, it is rather from this point on that Job himself seems to reply, in the verses that follow.

Job answered and said: Why then should I be judged, warned and rebuked by the Lord, hearing such things, since I am nothing? That is: why then should I bring judgment on myself by contradicting the Lord when he warns and reproves me? Hearing such things: that is, understanding how much justice and mercy there is in the way he deals with me, since of myself I am certainly nothing. What answer shall I give? That is: what could I say against the truth? I will put my hand over my mouth: that is, I will hold back and restrain my talkativeness. I have spoken once; I will not add a second time. Unless this is taken in a mystical sense, how did Job, who spoke so many times, speak only once? Or how will he not add a second time, when he is about to speak again shortly after? Rather, speaking here must be understood as the soul going out into these outward things, by which it abandons God and resists him. That is why Scripture calls a greater going-out of this kind a cry, when God says that the cry of Sodom has reached him. The opposite of this speaking and crying is that most blessed silence of which it is said: and he will be quiet, without fear of any evil. So he rightly says that he spoke once, in a single continuous speaking throughout the whole life of the old man, when he was a spirit that goes out and does not return. But now, putting his hand over his mouth so as to go out no further, he promises not to add a second time, so that he may not depart from God. Amen.
